# Locality Guide: Arkansas Post / Spanish Arkansas (to 1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post was established by the French in 1686, per Wikipedia, and lay in the lower Mississippi Valley. After the 1763 Treaty of Paris, Spain administered the territory until secretly retroceding it to France in 1800; the 1803 Louisiana Purchase brought it under the United States.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post itself was the sole organized settlement and seat of civil/military authority in this period — there was no "Arkansas County" in the modern sense yet.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Under Spain, Arkansas Post fell within the Spanish Louisiana administration, governed from New Orleans/St. Louis (Upper Louisiana); modern FamilySearch resolves "Arkansas" only as the post-1836 U.S. state (`standardPlace: "Arkansas, United States"`, dateRange +1836/), so none of the place tools have records specific to the colonial era — reported as a gap below.
- **Economy:** Fur trade and small-scale farming around the military/trading post.
- **Ethnic composition:** French and Spanish colonists, Native American (Quapaw) population in close contact with the post.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic missionaries served the post from the early 1700s onward (FamilySearch Wiki search result).
- **Key historical events:** Spanish administration 1763–1800; secret retrocession to France in 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803.

## Boundary changes
- No stable "Arkansas" jurisdiction existed as such before 1800 — the standardized place "Arkansas, United States" only dates from statehood in 1836 per `place_search`. Records from this period were created under French, then Spanish, colonial administration and are not filed under any U.S. county. Treat Arkansas Post as a single, continuous research subject whose records later ended up scattered among Spanish, French, and (eventually) American custodians — not as records that can be looked up under a modern Arkansas county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No U.S. civil registration applies to this period; Spain and France did not operate separate civil vital registration here — the church was the vital-records keeper.
- **What exists:** Sacramental registers functioned as vital records (see Church records below).
- **Where held:** See Church records.
- **Gaps:** No distinct civil vital-records series for the colonial period was located by any tool in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (French missionaries from the early 1700s, continuing under Spanish administration).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials, recorded for both European settlers and Native Americans, per a FamilySearch Wiki search hit ("Arkansas Genealogy," Church Records section): https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records
- **Where held:** That same wiki excerpt states surviving registers are held by the Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, with transcribed copies at the Arkansas History Commission. `volume_search` also located a FamilySearch-digitized volume: image group **008814402**, 64 images, coverage "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)," Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas, United States, date range **1763–1800**, language **Spanish (es)**.
- **Gaps:** This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it is browse-only, image-by-image, and in Spanish; a researcher must read Spanish to use it. `catalog_search({ standardPlace: "Arkansas, United States" })` returned **0 hits**, so no additional Catalog-listed microfilm or finding aid for this period was found — a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist (direct wiki references above show they do).
- **Language:** Spanish (confirmed by `volume_search`); earlier French-era entries may be in French (not confirmed by any tool here).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None — Arkansas fell outside the 1790–1800 U.S. federal censuses.
- **Other enumerations:** A FamilySearch Wiki search hit states that Spanish administration kept censuses ("padrones") at the post, held at the Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville), with microfilm at the Library of Congress: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records. No volume or collection for these padrones was found in `volume_search` or `collections_search` — not yet digitized by FamilySearch as far as this survey could confirm.
- **Access:** Not digitized/indexed per this survey; physical/archival only.

### Probate and court records
- Not addressed by any tool result for this period; this survey did not confirm their existence or location for Spanish-era Arkansas Post. Spanish colonial administration generally generated notarial and judicial records, but none specific to Arkansas Post surfaced here.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The same wiki search hit states Spanish administration issued land concessions, recorded with the colonial papers described above (Arkansas History Commission / Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress microfilm).
- **Date range:** 1763–1800 (Spanish period).
- **Where held:** As above; not separately confirmed in `collections_search` or `volume_search`.

### Military records
- The post was a Spanish military installation; no specific service or muster records for this period were returned by any tool in this survey. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/, from `external_links_search`) is the general U.S. repository for later military records but does not hold Spanish colonial military records.

### Cemetery, newspaper, immigration, and tax records
- No tool result in this survey returned anything specific to Arkansas Post for 1686–1800 in these categories. Newspapers.com and Find A Grave (below) are general national resources, not period-specific finds.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Digitized volume 008814402, "Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial)," Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 (browse-only, Spanish) | Fills the church baptism/marriage/burial gap for the Spanish period | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` for Arkansas, 1700–1800, returned exactly **1** matching volume (008814402); no `nextPageToken` was returned, so this is the complete matching set for that query. `collections_search` returned 3 Arkansas collections, but all three (county marriages 1837–1957, Freedmen's Bureau 1865–1872, census substitutes index 1819–1870) fall after 1800 and are not relevant to this period — a coverage gap for the colonial era specifically. `catalog_search` for "Arkansas, United States" returned 0 hits.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) | Transcribed Spanish colonial censuses (padrones), land concessions, and transcribed church registers, per FamilySearch Wiki search result | In-person or written request |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial administrative records, including censuses, per FamilySearch Wiki search result | In-person or written request to the Spanish national archive |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm of the above colonial records, per FamilySearch Wiki search result | In-person or interlibrary loan |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original (or earliest-surviving) sacramental registers for Arkansas Post, per FamilySearch Wiki search result | Written request to diocesan archives |

## Records NOT online
- The Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) and land concessions described in the FamilySearch Wiki search result are not present in any `collections_search` or `volume_search` result in this survey — they exist only in the physical/microfilm repositories named above.
- Any probate, notarial, or military service records that may exist for Spanish-period Arkansas Post were not located by any tool and are not confirmed online or in the Catalog.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that any of these Arkansas Post colonial record series were destroyed or lost. Where specific holdings are stated, they are per the FamilySearch Wiki search excerpt cited above; this survey found no statement of loss to report.

## Research tips
- The browse-only Spanish-language sacramental register volume (008814402, 1763–1800) has no name index — you must read through all 64 images yourself, and you will need some reading knowledge of Spanish (or paleography help) for entries in that era's hand.
- Because FamilySearch's place system only recognizes "Arkansas, United States" from 1836 onward, searches by modern standardized place will miss colonial-era materials; search by the historic name "Arkansas Post" directly, as done in this survey's wiki search, not by the modern state entry alone.
- Follow up directly with the Arkansas History Commission, the Archivo General de Indias (Seville), and the Library of Congress microfilm holdings named in the FamilySearch Wiki search result, since none of these colonial censuses, land concessions, or diocesan originals are digitized on FamilySearch.
- The generic FamilySearch Wiki jurisdiction pages (`getting_started`, `online_records`, `research_tips`, and the constructed `Arkansas_Vital_Records` URL) all returned only generic template content, not Arkansas-specific text, in this survey — they could not be used as a source for any Arkansas-specific claim and are flagged here as a page-coverage gap rather than cited for facts they don't contain.
- `catalog_search` returned 0 hits for "Arkansas, United States" — treat this as a cataloguing gap, not proof no colonial-era materials survive, since the Wiki search result above shows material does exist.

---
I looked into records surviving from the Arkansas Post area from before 1800, when the region was under Spanish rule. The main find is a set of old Catholic Church sacramental books (baptisms, marriages, burials) covering 1763 to 1800, which FamilySearch has photographed but not indexed by name and which are written in Spanish, so you would need to look through the images page by page; copies or related colonial-era census and land records are described as being held by the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock, the Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, the Spanish national archive in Seville, and on microfilm at the Library of Congress, though none of those specific items could be confirmed as available online. The standard FamilySearch place pages for "Arkansas" only cover the area from 1836 onward and gave no useful colonial-era detail, so this guide relies on a more targeted search instead.

Next, a research plan can be built around examining that Spanish-language sacramental register image by image and contacting the Arkansas History Commission and diocesan archives directly for the census and land records described above.

# Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory, United States (c. 1790, pre-statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Ohio did not exist as a jurisdiction in 1790. The region was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. FamilySearch's place record for "Ohio, United States" only begins in **1803** (at statehood) — a tool-level confirmation that no jurisdiction named "Ohio" existed in 1790.

- **Washington County** was organized in 1788 — the first county in the territory
- **Hamilton County** followed in 1790
- Both were carved out of the Northwest Territory under federal authority

---

## Boundary Changes

This is an evolving, progressively subdivided territory, not a simple rename:

- Records before county organization were generated at the **Northwest Territory** level
- Which county (if any) held jurisdiction over a specific 1790 location depends on its exact location
- Two separate land-grant systems operated here and must be searched **separately**:
  - **Virginia Military District** — metes-and-bounds surveys for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans; records held at the **Virginia State Library**
  - **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio) — grid survey; records held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society** in Cleveland
- Always search under "Northwest Territory," not "Ohio," for anything before 1803

---

## Available Records

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (collection 1542187) — covers 1790 directly
- **Digitized volume:** *Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799* (image group 005112233, 51 images, **0% name-indexed**) — must be browsed page by page, no name search possible
- Treat this volume and the Washington County Tax Records (1799–1803) as one continuous trail for the same locality

### Tax Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (collection 1987542) — begins just after 1790
- **Digitized volume:** *Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803* (image group 005112240, 73 images, 12% indexed)

### Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785, ~3M people) — county-level, begins at the edge of this period

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (collection 2246917) — covers 1790 directly; likely your **best substitute** for missing vital registration in this era

### Death Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001" — begins decades after 1790; not useful for this period

### Census
- The 1790 federal census was taken, but no Northwest Territory–specific enumeration collection was confirmed by any search tool result; treat pre-1800 census coverage as **unconfirmed**

### Military Records
- Relevant conflict: Northwest Indian War (Ohio Country)
- No specific collection was returned; service and pension records for this era are held at **NARA**; Fold3 is a curated external resource for military records

### Probate & Court Records
- No territorial-era probate/court collection was found online; these records are described as held physically at the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus)

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Land (1787–1840), Church (1787–1950), Marriages (1789+), Tax (1800+) | Free |
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus) | Early territorial court and land records | In-person / written request |
| Virginia State Library | Virginia Military District land warrants | In-person / written request |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person / written request |
| NARA / Fold3 | Military service and pension records | Free/subscription |

---

## Known Gaps & Losses

- No confirmed civil vital registration start date for the territorial period — church records fill this gap
- Zero catalog hits for digitized/filmed territorial court or probate records — treat as physical-access-only until a catalog entry is found
- Empty results for pre-1800 census and early newspaper/cemetery collections — these are **coverage/digitization gaps**, not evidence of destruction

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search "Northwest Territory," not "Ohio"** for anything before 1803 — the FamilySearch place record for Ohio begins only at statehood
2. **Determine your ancestor's exact location** before searching land records — it determines whether you go to the Virginia State Library (Military District) or the Western Reserve Historical Society (Western Reserve)
3. **Church records** (1787–1950 collection) are your best proxy for missing birth/marriage/death documentation in this era
4. The two digitized FamilySearch volumes (territorial land records and Washington County tax records) form **one continuous record trail** — search both together despite the different place names in the catalog
5. A research plan built around pinning down the exact township or county will unlock more precise record sets than a general Ohio search

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860, Gold Rush Era)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Statehood:** California was admitted to the Union in 1850, skipping organized-territory status entirely.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Previously Mexican territory until the 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
- **Key hubs:** San Francisco and Sacramento were the principal Gold Rush-era administrative and commercial centers.
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominated 1848–1855, driving massive transient migration, predominantly male.
- **Migration character:** Arrivals came from across the U.S. and abroad — a highly diverse, mobile population.

## Boundary Notes
California's county boundaries were repeatedly subdivided throughout the 1850s–1860s as population surged. Records before 1850 were created under Mexican and mission-era administration, not U.S. civil jurisdictions.

---

## Available Record Types

### Federal & State Census
| Record | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| 1850 Federal Census | First U.S. census taken in California — **partially destroyed**, some county returns missing | Ancestry, FamilySearch |
| **California State Census, 1850–1852** | Strong substitute for the federal gaps — **88% name-indexed and full-text searchable** | FamilySearch (image group 006601001) |

> **Key tip:** Because the 1850 federal census is incomplete for California, the 1850–1852 state census is your most important backup tool for this period.

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Births:** "California, County Births, 1850–1919" — FamilySearch collection id **2017276** (789,456 people)
- **Marriages:** "California, County Marriages, 1850–1952" — FamilySearch collection id **1452832** (1,135,780 people)
- **Deaths:** No death-record collection for this early period was found — a confirmed gap in this survey.
- **Pre-statehood alternative:** Franciscan mission registers (1769–1834) recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials before U.S. civil registration began. Searchable via FamilySearch collection "California, Mission Records, 1769–1850" (id **1804372**, 98,765 people).

---

### Gold Rush–Specific Records

**Mining Claim Registers (San Francisco, 1849–1855)**
- FamilySearch image group **006601002** — 340 images
- ⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse only**, page by page
- Original records held at county recorders' offices

**Port Arrival Registers (Sacramento, 1849–1858)**
- FamilySearch image group **006601003** — 298 images
- ⚠️ 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — **browse only**, page by page
- Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the **National Archives, San Bruno** — examine full manifests for all family members

**Overland Trail Diaries & Journals**
- Cited by the FamilySearch Wiki ("California Genealogy," Gold Rush Records section) as a migration-documentation source — not confirmed digitized

---

### Church Records
- Franciscan Catholic missions operated 1769–1834 — baptisms, marriages, burials recorded in Spanish.
- No Gold Rush-era (1848–1860) Protestant or other denominational register collections were returned by this survey — a coverage gap to investigate further.

---

### Voter Registration (Great Registers)
- "California, Great Registers, 1866–1910" — FamilySearch collection id **1923340** (1,345,678 people)
- Postdates the target window (registers began 1866) but highly useful to trace miners who stayed and settled in California.

---

### Probate, Land, and Court Records
- No online collections confirmed for this period by this survey — these are likely **physical-only** at county courthouses or state archives.
- Consult individual county recorders' offices for land and mining claim records.

---

### Newspapers
- No confirmed online Gold Rush–era California newspaper collection found by this survey.
- **Newspapers.com** is a curated external link for this place.

---

### Cemetery Records
- No confirmed online cemetery-record collection for this place/period.
- **Find A Grave** (`https://www.findagrave.com/`) covers California broadly.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key California Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | State census (1850–52), county births/marriages, mission records, Great Registers, mining claims (browse-only), port arrivals (browse-only) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census; other record types | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Ship passenger manifests, military records | Free/in-person |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **National Archives, San Bruno** | Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals |
| **California State Library** | Extensive Gold Rush–era manuscript collections |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush–era manuscript collections |
| **County recorders' offices** | Original mining claim records, land records |

---

## Known Record Losses
- The **1850 federal census for California was partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing entirely.
- The **1850–1852 California State Census** (88% indexed, full-text searchable) is the best substitute.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1850–1852 state census** — it's more complete than the federal census for California in this period and is name-indexed.
2. **Mine the Gold Rush-specific records:** Browse the mining claim registers and Sacramento port arrival registers image by image (neither is name-indexed).
3. **Ship passenger lists at NARA San Bruno** cover San Francisco arrivals — examine the full manifest, not just the head of household.
4. **Population was overwhelmingly male and transient** — search for men traveling alone, not in family groups.
5. **Pre-1848 ancestors** will appear only in Franciscan mission registers (1769–1834), not civil records.
6. **For settlers who stayed:** The Great Registers (voter registration, starting 1866) are a powerful tool to locate men once they put down roots.
7. **Physical archives are essential** for probate, land, and court records — county courthouses, the California State Library, and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley are the key repositories.

---

*Survey note: This guide covers California statewide for approximately 1848–1860. Several attempted lookups of California's own detailed FamilySearch Wiki guidance pages returned only a generic fallback rather than California-specific content — treat registration start dates and some details as unconfirmed, and verify directly at the [FamilySearch California Genealogy Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records).*

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York — Colonial Period (1700s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- New York City has been continuously settled from the Dutch period (1624 onward). Throughout the 1700s it falls under the **Province of New York** (British colonial, 1664–1783) — "New York" as a state doesn't begin until 1788.
- The city transitioned from Dutch (New Amsterdam) to English rule in 1664. Its population was mixed Dutch and English; it served as a major commercial port and administrative center.
- Dominant religious denominations: **Dutch Reformed**, **Anglican (Trinity Church)**, and **Presbyterian** — all kept registers that substitute for the civil registration that didn't exist in this era.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for vital registration)*
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776** — baptisms, marriages, and burials. One digitized volume confirmed online at FamilySearch (image group 007733180, 211 images). **Important cautions:** 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, must be browsed image by image, and are written in **Dutch**.
- **Anglican (Trinity Church) and Presbyterian registers** — referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki as existing, but no digitized collection was confirmed by this survey. Likely available only through physical archives.
- There was **no civil vital registration** in colonial New York — church registers are the primary substitutes for births, marriages, and deaths.

### Probate & Court Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971" (collection id 1542780) covers the full 1700s.
- Colonial wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**; published *Abstracts of Wills* from the New-York Historical Society index these.
- Mayor's Court records referenced narratively but not confirmed digitized.

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630–1975" (collection id 2078654) spans the 1700s.
- Covers deeds, grants, and patents from the colonial period.

### Tax Records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804" (collection id 1678432) reaches only the very end of the century.
- Colonial tax assessment lists for earlier years and specific wards are referenced as existing, but not confirmed digitized — useful as a **census substitute** where available.

### Church Records (FamilySearch)
- **FamilySearch Collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640–1940" (collection id 1469062) — broader church records collection.

### Census Records
- **No colonial census** was returned for the 1700s. The U.S. federal census begins in 1790 (at the very end of this period). Tax lists and militia rolls serve as census-adjacent substitutes.

### Military Records
- Colonial **militia rolls** are referenced by the FamilySearch Wiki but not confirmed as digitized in this survey.

### Immigration Records
- As a major colonial port, NYC generated passenger arrival records, but no specific 1700s collection was confirmed digitized by this survey. NARA is a general starting point.

### Newspapers & Cemetery Records
- Generic links to Newspapers.com and Find A Grave were returned, but no colonial-NYC-specific title or coverage was confirmed.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1640–1940; Land Records 1630–1975; Probate Records 1629–1971; Tax Rolls 1799–1804; Dutch Reformed image volume 1700–1776 (browse-only, Dutch) |
| **Ancestry** | General U.S. collections; post-1790 census |
| **Fold3** | General military records (no colonial NYC confirmed) |
| **NARA** | Federal records generally; check for colonial-era holdings |

### Physical / Archival
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills* series; extensive colonial-era collections |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** | Extensive colonial-era research collections |
| **New York State Archives** | New York Colonial Manuscripts; Mayor's Court records |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Plan for Dutch-language records.** The Dutch Reformed Church registers (the most digitized source for this period) are written in Dutch and are not name-indexed — you'll need to browse them page by page and either read Dutch or get the pages translated.

2. **Check the published *Abstracts of Wills*.** The New-York Historical Society's published index covers wills proved in the colonial Prerogative Court — check it before assuming no will survives for your ancestor.

3. **Search as "colonial/provincial New York," not "State of New York."** New York statehood begins in 1788, so catalog and collection searches framed as the Province of New York will find colonial-era records more reliably.

4. **Tax lists as census substitutes.** No 1700s census exists; tax assessment lists and militia rolls (where available) can help locate households.

5. **Anglican and Presbyterian registers are likely archival-only.** Trinity Church (Anglican) and Presbyterian registers were not found as digitized collections in this survey — contact the denominational archives and the New-York Historical Society directly.

6. **FamilySearch catalog returned no hits** for New York City in this survey — that's a cataloguing gap in the tool, not proof that no holdings exist. Consult the physical repositories above directly.

---

The colonial period in New York City is research-rich but presents real hurdles: no civil registration, Dutch-language church registers that must be read page by page, and several important record series (Anglican/Presbyterian registers, militia rolls, colonial tax lists) that exist physically but are not yet fully digitized. Start with the Dutch Reformed Church registers and the probate/land FamilySearch collections, and plan on archival visits or requests to the New-York Historical Society and New York State Archives for records not yet online. If you'd like, I can build a sequenced research plan from here.

- **Key historical events:** Dutch rule 1626–1664; English seizure and renaming in 1664; city served as capital of the Province of New York and briefly as the first U.S. capital (Wikipedia, above).

## Boundary changes
- New York City's own standard-place record runs continuously from 1624, with no county-level restructuring noted by the tools in this survey during the 1700s.

No comparable Anglican or Presbyterian volume turned up in `volume_search` for this place/period — that is a digitization gap, not evidence the records don't exist; the FamilySearch Wiki search result above points to Trinity Church (Anglican) and Presbyterian registers as existing but not confirmed digitized here.

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies, transitioning to an independent state during this period.
- Research is organized by county; county-level research is recommended for most record types.
- Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony, and major engagements — including the Siege of Yorktown (1781) — occurred on Virginia soil.

---

## Military Records (Primary Focus)

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- **Collection 1945678** — "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783" (345,678 persons indexed)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678
  Name-indexed and searchable.

**Browse-Only Volume:**
- **Image group 005301447** — "Revolutionary War land bounty warrants," Virginia, 1779–1800 (341 images, 0% name-indexed)
  Must be browsed image by image — not searchable by name.

**FamilySearch Wiki findings:**
- Continental Line service records and muster rolls → **NARA, Record Group 93**
- Virginia militia records → **Library of Virginia, Richmond**
- Pension and bounty-land warrant applications → **NARA, Record Group 15**
- Post-war bounty lands were granted in the Virginia Military District of Ohio; warrant/survey records connecting veterans to those claims are at the **Virginia State Library**

**Fold3** (subscription): https://www.fold3.com/ — digitized pension and service record images drawn from NARA holdings

---

## Church Records
- **Collection 1598230** — "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929" (1,234,567 persons)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
  Spans the 1775–1783 window.

---

## Census / Tax Records (Substitute for Lost 1790 Census)
- The **1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed** (burned in the War of 1812 fires). County tax lists from the 1780s are the standard substitute.
- **Image group 005301449** — "State enumerations / tax lists," Virginia, 1782–1799 (87 images, full-text searchable but not name-indexed)
- **Collection 1456723** — "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850" (456,789 persons, indexed)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723

---

## Court & Probate Records
- County court order books frequently record militia musters, oaths of allegiance, and wartime supply claims — not just civil suits.
- **Image group 005301448** — Augusta County, Virginia, court order books, 1775–1795 (158 images, 61% name-indexed)
- **Collection 2134567** — "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920" (1,789,012 persons)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567

---

## Land Records
- **Collection 1734285** — "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900" (2,567,890 persons)
  → https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285
- Revolutionary War land bounty warrants also link veterans to later Ohio land claims (Virginia Military District of Ohio).

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Indexed military, church, land, court, and tax collections (all above) | Free |
| Fold3 | Digitized pension/service record images | Subscription |
| NARA (National Archives) | Continental Line muster rolls (RG 93); pension/bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free |
| Library of Virginia, Richmond | Virginia militia records | In-person / written request |
| Virginia State Library | Bounty-land warrant and survey records (Ohio land claims) | In-person / written request |
| County courthouses | Original court order books, deeds, probate | In-person / mail |

---

## Records NOT Online
- The land bounty warrant image volume (005301447) has no name index — must be browsed page by page.
- Original Continental Line muster rolls are held at NARA (RG 93) and are not confirmed as fully digitized.

---

## Known Record Losses
- The **1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed**. Use county tax lists (1782–1799) as the primary substitute for census-era family reconstruction.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Tax lists as a census substitute** — The 1782–1799 state tax list volume (image group 005301449, full-text searchable) and the indexed tax records collection (1456723) are your best tools for placing a family in a county during and just after the war.
2. **County court order books** — These often record militia musters, oaths of loyalty, and wartime claims. Augusta County's are 61% indexed; other county volumes should be targeted separately.
3. **Search neighboring jurisdictions** — Wartime service and land bounties often crossed what are today separate states. Check Maryland, North Carolina, and especially Kentucky and West Virginia (both then part of Virginia).
4. **FamilySearch Catalog gap** — A subject-filtered catalog search for "Revolutionary War" at the Virginia state level returned no hits in this survey. Retry with a specific county name or regiment for better results.
5. **Next step** — Once you identify a specific county or ancestor, run a county-level locality guide and a research plan to sequence your searches.

## Records NOT online
The browse-only bounty warrant volume (image group 005301447, 341 images, 1779–1800) has no name index online — these must be browsed image by image. No tool result in this survey located original Continental Line muster rolls online; per the wiki-search snippet they are held at NARA (RG 93).

**Disaster Losses and Record Survival in Early New Orleans**

New Orleans suffered two devastating fires — in **1788** and **1794** — that destroyed much of the French Quarter and many early civil records. Subsequent hurricanes, floods, and yellow fever outbreaks caused further archival damage over the years.

**What survived and where to look:**

1. **St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers** — Baptisms, marriages, and burials going back to **1731** (with some gaps) survived the fires and remain the primary substitute for lost vital records. A small digitized set covering **1803–1820** exists online, but it is unindexed and partly in French, requiring page-by-page browsing. The bulk of the collection remains onsite in New Orleans.

3. **Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)** — Holds additional state-level records that may serve as substitutes or complements.

**Practical caveats:** Several FamilySearch Wiki pages with more detail on this topic could not be fully retrieved during this survey, so some specifics should be verified directly on the wiki. The notarial archive's online portion has no name index and is partly in French.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by the French; passed to Spain 1763, back to France 1803, then to the US via the Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the parish seat of Orleans Parish (Louisiana uses parishes, not counties).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States.
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed -- place_population returned no data for this place/period in this survey.
- **Economy:** Port city economy; river/maritime trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** French, Spanish, Creole, Acadian, and enslaved and free people of color populations under French/Spanish/American successive rule (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church dominant (St. Louis Cathedral); other denominations present later.
- **Key historical events:** Devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result).

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans/Orleans Parish has been a stable jurisdiction since French founding; Louisiana itself changed sovereignty (French to Spanish to French to American) between 1763 and 1803, and became a US state in 1812 -- records from the colonial period were created under French and Spanish civil-law administration, not American county government.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed for Louisiana/Orleans Parish in this survey -- the FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Vital_Records page could not be read (only generic fallback content returned); do not assume a date.
- **What exists:** For 1800-1830, civil vital registration as commonly understood in American states is not confirmed; sacramental (church) registers served this function.
- **Where held:** Unconfirmed at state/parish level in this survey.
- **Gaps:** 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed much of the colonial-era civil record base (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search snippet).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) dominant for this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps), per the FamilySearch Wiki search result (New Orleans Genealogy, 'Records Surviving Disasters').
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral archives (repository not independently confirmed by a direct wiki_read in this survey -- carried from the wiki_search snippet only).
- **Gaps:** Known gaps in the sacramental registers are noted by the same source but not itemized by year in this survey -- the FamilySearch Wiki page itself could not be read directly.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for the colonial period (consistent with the fr/en languages flagged on the one digitized volume found, below).

### Court and notarial records
- **Types:** Notarial acts are central under Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system; successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions are the Louisiana-specific equivalents of probate/guardianship records (FamilySearch Wiki search result).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, which holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result. This is named by that source as an original-custodian repository for notarial acts, not a derivative index.
- **Note:** One digitized volume was found via volume_search (image group 004990115, 167 images, coverage 1803-1820, 'Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)', languages French and English) -- 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, so it must be browsed image by image with no search, and partly in French.

### Probate records
- A collections_search hit, 'Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984' (collection 2078341, ~456,789 people), overlaps this period and is held by FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed collection); underlying original successions records are a Louisiana civil-law court record, not confirmed to a specific repository in this survey.

### Census records
- Federal decennial census from 1790 applies generally, per FamilySearch's generic guidance; no New Orleans/Louisiana-specific 1800-1830 schedule coverage or gaps were confirmed in this survey (catalog_search returned 0 hits; place_population returned no data).

### Land records
- Spanish and French colonial land grants predate the American rectangular survey system; the US holds federal land records for areas surveyed after the Louisiana Purchase. No Louisiana-specific land office or survey-system detail was confirmed in this survey (the Louisiana_Land_and_Property wiki page was not fetched).

### Military records
- War of 1812 (including the Battle of New Orleans, 1815) falls in this window; NARA holds federal service and pension records. No Louisiana-specific collection was confirmed in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- Not confirmed in this survey; no tool result named a specific early-1800s New Orleans newspaper title or archive.

### Immigration/emigration records
- New Orleans was a major port of entry in this period; passenger lists and naturalization records would exist at NARA, but no New Orleans-specific collection, date range, or count was confirmed by a tool result in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 people); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 people); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 people) | Substitutes for lost civil vital/court records destroyed in the 1788/1794 fires | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | General census gap-filling | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Burial/cemetery substitute source | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituary/legal-notice substitute | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 service/pension gap | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Passenger lists, naturalization, federal land, military | Free/in-person & online |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one digitized volume (image group 004990115) was returned by volume_search for this place and period; it is not stated to be the complete set of surviving material -- treat it as a sample, not exhaustive.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (original custodian per the FamilySearch Wiki search result) | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral | Sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps) | In-person / written request (not independently confirmed by direct wiki_read) |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives' 30 million pages of notarial acts are not stated to be online in this survey -- only one 1803-1820 microfilm-derived volume (browse-only, partly French) was found via volume_search.
- Sacramental registers predating full online digitization are not confirmed online beyond the FamilySearch Church Records collection noted above.

## Known record losses
- The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed much of the French Quarter and "many colonial records," per Wikipedia and the FamilySearch Wiki search result -- this is cited context for the record class broadly (colonial-era civil/municipal records), not a claim that any specific named record series was destroyed. No tool result in this survey itemized which specific registers or series did or did not survive.
- Repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods are stated by Wikipedia to have "further damaged archival holdings," but no tool result specifies which records or years this affected.
- Substitute sources identified by the same source: St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (from 1731) and the Notarial Archives (acts from 1734).

## Research tips
- For 1800-1830 New Orleans, treat St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and notarial acts as the backbone sources, since civil vital registration for this period is not confirmed and much colonial civil record-keeping was damaged by the 1788/1794 fires (FamilySearch Wiki search result, 'New Orleans Genealogy', https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Louisiana's civil-law system means successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions are the research-relevant equivalents of common-law probate/guardianship records -- search under these terms, not just 'probate' or 'guardianship' (same source, 'Louisiana Genealogy', https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- The direct FamilySearch Wiki pages for New Orleans Genealogy, Louisiana Genealogy, and Louisiana Vital Records could not be read as their specific articles in this survey (only generic fallback content came back) -- re-run this survey, or fetch those URLs again later, before relying on their absence of further detail.
- The one digitized notarial-acts volume found (1803-1820, image group 004990115) is 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, and partly in French -- budget time to browse it image by image and to read French-language entries.
- Check both the Notarial Archives Research Center and the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge, since early territorial and state records are held separately from the city's notarial acts.

# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by the French; passed to Spain 1763, back to France 1803, then to the US via the Louisiana Purchase 1803; Louisiana became a state in 1812.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans is itself the parish seat of Orleans Parish (Louisiana uses parishes, not counties).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Louisiana, United States.
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed -- place_population returned no data for this place/period in this survey.
- **Economy:** Port city economy; river/maritime trade.
- **Ethnic composition:** French, Spanish, Creole, Acadian, and enslaved and free people of color populations under French/Spanish/American successive rule (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic Church dominant (St. Louis Cathedral); other denominations present later.
- **Key historical events:** Devastating fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed much of the colonial-era built environment and many records; repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods further damaged archival holdings (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result).

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans/Orleans Parish has been a stable jurisdiction since French founding; Louisiana itself changed sovereignty (French to Spanish to French to American) between 1763 and 1803, and became a US state in 1812 -- records from the colonial period were created under French and Spanish civil-law administration, not American county government.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed for Louisiana/Orleans Parish in this survey -- the FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana_Vital_Records page could not be read (only generic fallback content returned); do not assume a date.
- **What exists:** For 1800-1830, civil vital registration as commonly understood in American states is not confirmed; sacramental (church) registers served this function.
- **Where held:** Unconfirmed at state/parish level in this survey.
- **Gaps:** 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed much of the colonial-era civil record base (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search snippet).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials, from 1731, with gaps) are the primary substitute, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (St. Louis Cathedral) dominant for this period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731 (with gaps), per the FamilySearch Wiki search result (New Orleans Genealogy, 'Records Surviving Disasters').
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral archives (repository not independently confirmed by a direct wiki_read in this survey -- carried from the wiki_search snippet only).
- **Gaps:** Known gaps in the sacramental registers are noted by the same source but not itemized by year in this survey -- the FamilySearch Wiki page itself could not be read directly.
- **Language:** French and Spanish for the colonial period (consistent with the fr/en languages flagged on the one digitized volume found, below).

### Court and notarial records
- **Types:** Notarial acts are central under Louisiana's civil-law (Napoleonic Code) system; successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions are the Louisiana-specific equivalents of probate/guardianship records (FamilySearch Wiki search result).
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center, which holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result. This is named by that source as an original-custodian repository for notarial acts, not a derivative index.
- **Note:** One digitized volume was found via volume_search (image group 004990115, 167 images, coverage 1803-1820, 'Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)', languages French and English) -- 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, so it must be browsed image by image with no search, and partly in French.

### Probate records
- A collections_search hit, 'Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984' (collection 2078341, ~456,789 people), overlaps this period and is held by FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (indexed collection); underlying original successions records are a Louisiana civil-law court record, not confirmed to a specific repository in this survey.

### Census records
- Federal decennial census from 1790 applies generally, per FamilySearch's generic guidance; no New Orleans/Louisiana-specific 1800-1830 schedule coverage or gaps were confirmed in this survey (catalog_search returned 0 hits; place_population returned no data).

### Land records
- Spanish and French colonial land grants predate the American rectangular survey system; the US holds federal land records for areas surveyed after the Louisiana Purchase. No Louisiana-specific land office or survey-system detail was confirmed in this survey (the Louisiana_Land_and_Property wiki page was not fetched).

### Military records
- War of 1812 (including the Battle of New Orleans, 1815) falls in this window; NARA holds federal service and pension records. No Louisiana-specific collection was confirmed in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- Not confirmed in this survey; no tool result named a specific early-1800s New Orleans newspaper title or archive.

### Immigration/emigration records
- New Orleans was a major port of entry in this period; passenger lists and naturalization records would exist at NARA, but no New Orleans-specific collection, date range, or count was confirmed by a tool result in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925 (987,654 people); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984 (456,789 people); Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819-1964 (2,345,678 people) | Substitutes for lost civil vital/court records destroyed in the 1788/1794 fires | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | General census gap-filling | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Burial/cemetery substitute source | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (https://www.newspapers.com/) | Obituary/legal-notice substitute | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | War of 1812 service/pension gap | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Passenger lists, naturalization, federal land, military | Free/in-person & online |

**Coverage of this survey:** Only one digitized volume (image group 004990115) was returned by volume_search for this place and period; it is not stated to be the complete set of surviving material -- treat it as a sample, not exhaustive.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734 (original custodian per the FamilySearch Wiki search result) | In-person / written request |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans / St. Louis Cathedral | Sacramental registers from 1731 (with gaps) | In-person / written request (not independently confirmed by direct wiki_read) |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early state records, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result | In-person / mail |

## Records NOT online
- The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives' 30 million pages of notarial acts are not stated to be online in this survey -- only one 1803-1820 microfilm-derived volume (browse-only, partly French) was found via volume_search.
- Sacramental registers predating full online digitization are not confirmed online beyond the FamilySearch Church Records collection noted above.

## Known record losses
- The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed much of the French Quarter and "many colonial records," per Wikipedia and the FamilySearch Wiki search result -- this is cited context for the record class broadly (colonial-era civil/municipal records), not a claim that any specific named record series was destroyed. No tool result in this survey itemized which specific registers or series did or did not survive.
- Repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and floods are stated by Wikipedia to have "further damaged archival holdings," but no tool result specifies which records or years this affected.
- Substitute sources identified by the same source: St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (from 1731) and the Notarial Archives (acts from 1734).

## Research tips
- For 1800-1830 New Orleans, treat St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers and notarial acts as the backbone sources, since civil vital registration for this period is not confirmed and much colonial civil record-keeping was damaged by the 1788/1794 fires (FamilySearch Wiki search result, 'New Orleans Genealogy', https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters).
- Louisiana's civil-law system means successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), and interdictions are the research-relevant equivalents of common-law probate/guardianship records -- search under these terms, not just 'probate' or 'guardianship' (same source, 'Louisiana Genealogy', https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System).
- The direct FamilySearch Wiki pages for New Orleans Genealogy, Louisiana Genealogy, and Louisiana Vital Records could not be read as their specific articles in this survey (only generic fallback content came back) -- re-run this survey, or fetch those URLs again later, before relying on their absence of further detail.
- The one digitized notarial-acts volume found (1803-1820, image group 004990115) is 0% indexed, not full-text searchable, and partly in French -- budget time to browse it image by image and to read French-language entries.
- Check both the Notarial Archives Research Center and the Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge, since early territorial and state records are held separately from the city's notarial acts.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — 1840s Immigration Research

## Overview

Boston was one of the major U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving massive numbers of Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born. Here is what records and repositories can help trace ancestors arriving during this period.

---

## Key Record Types

### Passenger / Arrival Records
- **Customs passenger lists, Port of Boston, 1820–1891** — held in National Archives Record Group 36 at the **National Archives at Boston (Waltham)**. The 1840s-era lists typically recorded only name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin — far less detail than later Ellis Island manifests.
- On FamilySearch: **"Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"** (collection id 1784312). There is also a digitized volume specifically covering Port of Boston passenger lists for **1840–1850** (image group 003345210, 389 images), but it is only about 3% name-indexed — it must be browsed or searched via full text rather than a name index.

### Church Records
- Catholic parishes expanded rapidly with Irish immigration. **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's** are among Boston-area parishes with registers from the 1840s onward.
- The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds the originals.
- Also indexed on FamilySearch: **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection id 1921657).

### Civil Vital Records
- FamilySearch collection **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (id 2061550) covers this period. The exact year Massachusetts began mandatory civil registration for this city could not be confirmed through tools in this research run — verify this directly on the FamilySearch Wiki.
- For Irish Catholic families, parish registers are often the more reliable source for births, marriages, and deaths during the 1840s.

### Census Records
- The **1840 and 1850 U.S. federal censuses** both fall within your window and are essential anchors for locating immigrant households in Boston.

### Naturalization Records
- Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record (local, state, or federal), so they are scattered.
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906"** (id 1459213).
- National Archives (Waltham) holds originals for federal court naturalizations.

### Probate Records
- FamilySearch collection: **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (id 1678901), which spans the 1840s.

### Newspapers
- **The Pilot**, Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper, published arrival notices and **missing-persons advertisements** for the immigrant community — a distinctive and highly valuable source for this era and population.
- Newspapers.com covers some Boston-area papers; confirm specific titles through their search interface.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists, RG 36; federal naturalization records | In-person or written request |
| FamilySearch (online) | Passenger lists, church records, vital records, naturalization, probate | Free |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1840s onward | Contact archives directly |
| Suffolk County Courthouse / Massachusetts State Archives | Probate, court, and naturalization records | In-person or mail |
| Newspapers.com | Boston-area newspapers including The Pilot | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Don't rely on name indexes alone** for the Port of Boston passenger lists — the 1840–1850 volume is only 3% name-indexed. Use full-text search on FamilySearch or plan to browse images directly.
2. **Catholic parish registers are essential** for Irish immigrant families; don't skip them even if civil registration records seem available.
3. **Check The Pilot** for arrival and missing-persons notices — it was specifically aimed at Irish immigrants and carried information found nowhere else.
4. **Country of origin on 1840s manifests means Ireland, England, Germany, etc.** — not a specific town or county — so passenger lists alone rarely pinpoint an exact origin; they establish arrival and must be combined with parish and other records.
5. The FamilySearch Catalog search for passenger lists at this place returned no hits — a catalog gap, **not** evidence the records don't exist. Go directly to NARA Waltham's finding aids for RG 36 to confirm what is available.

# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (mid-1800s, c. 1830–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** Indian Territory was designated under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for relocated tribes, including the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole). Oklahoma did not become a state until 1907.
- **Administrative structure:** Governed through tribal nations and federal Indian agencies — no county system in this period.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions were established among the tribes from the 1820s onward (per FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records").

---

## Available Record Types

### Tribal Rolls and Treaty-Related Records *(most critical for this period)*
- **Early rolls confirmed:** Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) are key enrollment records predating the Dawes Rolls.
- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The most widely used tribal rolls, but postdate this period.
- **Digitized volume confirmed:** "Tribal Enrollment Cards," Indian Territory, 1840–1870 — image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable (FamilySearch).
- **Collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (FamilySearch collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people) — overlaps the target period from 1851 onward.
- **Original holdings:** Treaty documents, annuity rolls, and agency correspondence held by the Bureau of Indian Affairs / National Archives (NARA).

### Church / Mission Records
- Missionaries (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) kept registers of converts, students, and community members from the 1820s.
- **Collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (FamilySearch collection id 1654321, ~123,456 people).

### Land Records
- **Collection confirmed:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (FamilySearch collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people) — covers the full target period.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **None existed** in this period. Oklahoma was not a state; no territorial civil registration for births, marriages, or deaths was in place. Tribal rolls, mission registers, and federal agency records serve as substitutes.

### Census Records
- Standard federal census schedules did not enumerate most Indian Territory residents by name in this era. Tribal/agency rolls (above) are the period's census substitute.

### Military, Probate, Newspaper, Cemetery Records
- Not confirmed by tools for this specific period in Indian Territory. General resources (Fold3, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com) exist but no Oklahoma/Indian-Territory–specific holdings were returned.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Confirmed Holdings for This Place & Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | "Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (id 1987432); "Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (id 1654321); "Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (id 1541872); Tribal Enrollment Cards volume 002298871 | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Original BIA agency records, annuity rolls, treaty documents (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki) | Free (in-person / online) |
| **Tribal Nation Archives** | Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, etc. — nation-specific records not necessarily digitized elsewhere | Varies |
| Fold3 | General military records; no Oklahoma-specific holding confirmed | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | General newspaper archive; no Indian Territory–specific holding confirmed | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | General cemetery database; no Indian Territory–specific holding confirmed | Free |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852)** for mid-1800s ancestors — these predate the Dawes Rolls and are the relevant enrollment records for this era.
2. **Missionary registers are the primary vital-record substitute** — they may record births, marriages, deaths, and community membership not found anywhere else.
3. **FamilySearch Catalog:** The catalog search for Oklahoma returned 0 hits in this survey, which likely reflects a cataloging gap, not an absence of microfilm or manuscript holdings. Search the FamilySearch Catalog directly by tribal nation name (e.g., "Cherokee Nation," "Choctaw") for additional microfilm.
4. **BIA agency correspondence and school records** referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki were not matched to a specific online collection in this survey — treat these as likely NARA-held physical records requiring a direct NARA search.
5. **Tribal nation archives** (Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, etc.) hold nation-specific records not necessarily available through FamilySearch or NARA online — contact them directly.
6. The standard FamilySearch Wiki research-strategy pages for Oklahoma returned generic, non-place-specific content in this survey; consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for the article **"Oklahoma Native American Records"** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records) for deeper guidance.

---

**Summary:** Because Indian Territory was not a U.S. state in the mid-1800s, there are no ordinary birth, marriage, or death certificates from this era. The critical record classes are **tribal enrollment rolls** (Old Settler Cherokee Roll 1851, Drennen Roll 1852), **missionary church registers**, and **federal Indian-agency and land records**. Several of these have been digitized and indexed through FamilySearch; originals are held at the National Archives. A research plan can be built from this guide to target specific ancestors against these records.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The region was designated Indian Territory under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, used for forced relocation of tribes including the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole), per Wikipedia. Oklahoma did not become a state until 1907 (FamilySearch place record, type "State", date range from 1907).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not applicable in this period — government operated through tribal nations and federal Indian agencies rather than counties.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Administered as federal Indian Territory, not a state or organized county system, during the target period.
- **Population during period:** Could not be confirmed — `place_population` returned no data for this place/period in this survey.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by tool results in this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** Relocated Native nations (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole), per Wikipedia.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missions were established among the tribes from the 1820s onward, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result "Oklahoma Native American Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Trail of Tears relocation; subsequent treaty-based tribal governance, per Wikipedia.

## Boundary changes
- The area functioned as Indian Territory, not a state or county system, throughout the target period; it was not reorganized into the modern state/county structure until the 1890s–1907. No further boundary-change detail was confirmed by tools in this survey.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide or territorial civil registration existed in this period — Oklahoma was not a state until 1907, so births/marriages/deaths were not civilly registered at that level during the mid-1800s.
- **What exists:** None confirmed for this period at any civil level.
- **Where held:** N/A.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Tribal rolls, mission/church registers, and federal agency records (see below) substitute for vital records in this era.

### Tribal rolls and treaty-related records
- **What exists:** The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and the Drennen Roll (1852) are early tribal enrollment records for the Five Civilized Tribes; the later Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the most widely used but postdate this period — per FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- **Digitized holding confirmed by this survey:** `volume_search` found one digitized volume, "Tribal Enrollment Cards," covering Indian Territory, 1840–1870, image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable.
- **Also confirmed:** `collections_search` lists "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people) — overlaps the target period from 1851 onward.
- **Where held:** Treaty documents, annuity rolls, and agency correspondence are held by the Bureau of Indian Affairs/National Archives, per the same FamilySearch Wiki result.

### Church/mission records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian missions (from the 1820s), per FamilySearch Wiki ("Oklahoma Native American Records").
- **Record types:** Registers of converts, students, and community members kept by missionaries.
- **Where held:** `collections_search` confirms a digitized collection: "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection id 1654321, ~123,456 people), overlapping the target period.
- **Gaps:** Specific denomination-by-denomination survival was not confirmed by tools in this survey.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Standard federal census schedules did not enumerate most Indian Territory residents by name in this period in the way they did U.S. states; no Indian Territory-specific federal schedule was confirmed by tools here.
- **Other enumerations:** The tribal/agency rolls above (Old Settler Cherokee Roll 1851, Drennen Roll 1852, and the "Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection) function as the period's census substitute.
- **Access:** The Tribal Enrollment Cards volume is indexed and full-text searchable (see above); the "Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection is indexed per `collections_search`.

### Probate and court records
- Not confirmed by tools in this survey. Tribal nations maintained their own judicial systems in this period rather than U.S. county courts; no specific holdings were returned.

### Land records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` confirms "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people), which overlaps the full target period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by a `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` wiki page in this survey — the constructed wiki URL did not return Oklahoma-specific content (see Research tips gap note below).

### Military records
- Not confirmed by tools in this survey for this specific period; Fold3 is listed among externally curated military-record resources (see Repository guide), but no Indian-Territory-specific holding was returned.

### Cemetery records
- Find A Grave is listed as a curated external resource (see Repository guide); no Indian Territory-specific cemetery data was confirmed by tools in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com is listed as a curated external resource (see Repository guide); no specific title or date range for this place/period was confirmed.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not applicable in the usual port-of-entry sense; the relevant "migration" record set for this population is the forced-relocation and annuity/agency documentation discussed above, not passenger manifests.

### Tax records
- Not confirmed by tools in this survey.

### Other record types
- Federal Bureau of Indian Affairs agency correspondence and school records are referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki search result above but no specific digitized collection for them was returned by `collections_search` or `catalog_search` in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (id 1541872); "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (id 1987432); "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (id 1654321); digitized volume "Tribal Enrollment Cards," Indian Territory 1840-1870 (image group 002298871) | Tribal rolls, land records, and mission/church records for the period | Free |
| National Archives (NARA) | General reference only — listed as curated external link | Treaty documents and BIA agency records, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result | Free, in-person/online |
| Fold3 | General military-records collection, not Oklahoma-specific per this survey | Not tied to a confirmed Oklahoma-period gap | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | General newspaper collection, not Oklahoma-specific per this survey | Not tied to a confirmed Oklahoma-period gap | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | General cemetery database, not Oklahoma-specific per this survey | Not tied to a confirmed Oklahoma-period gap | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned only 1 matching digitized volume for "Indian Territory, United States," 1840–1870 — a complete result for that query, not a partial page. `catalog_search` on "Oklahoma, United States" returned 0 hits, which is a cataloging gap in this survey, not evidence that no microfilm or manuscript holdings exist.

### Physical repositories
- National Archives and Records Administration — holds original BIA agency records, annuity rolls, and treaty documents, per the FamilySearch Wiki search result cited above. No specific NARA branch/record-group number was confirmed by tools in this survey.
- Tribal nation archives (e.g., Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation) were not directly queried by any tool in this survey; their own archives commonly hold nation-specific record sets not necessarily digitized elsewhere.

## Records NOT online
- Full BIA agency correspondence and school records referenced in the FamilySearch Wiki search snippet were not matched to a specific online collection by `collections_search` or `catalog_search` in this survey — treat as likely physical-only/NARA-held unless a further catalog search finds them.

## Known record losses
- No record loss was stated by any tool result in this survey. None should be assumed.

## Research tips
- The Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851) and Drennen Roll (1852) predate the Dawes Rolls and are the relevant enrollment records for this mid-1800s period — per FamilySearch Wiki, "Oklahoma Native American Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls).
- Missionary registers (Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian) are a key substitute for vital records in this era — same source as above, "Missionary and Agency Records" section.
- **Gap encountered in this survey:** all four `wiki_place_page` sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) for "Oklahoma, United States" returned only a generic, non-place-specific template page, and the constructed `{Jurisdiction}_Indian_Records` wiki URL redirected to a similarly generic page — none of these could be cited for Oklahoma-specific research strategy. Re-running this survey, or consulting the FamilySearch Wiki directly for "Oklahoma Native American Records" and "Indian Territory," is recommended to fill this gap.
- `catalog_search` returned 0 hits for "Oklahoma, United States" — this is a cataloging gap in this survey, not proof that no microfilm, manuscript, or finding-aid holdings exist; a direct FamilySearch Catalog search by tribal nation name may surface more.
- `external_links_search` for this place returned only generic national-level resources (Ancestry census collection, NARA, Fold3, Newspapers.com, Find A Grave) rather than Oklahoma/Indian-Territory-specific curated links — treat these as general-purpose starting points only.

---
This survey looked at Indian Territory, the area that later became Oklahoma, for the years around 1830 to 1870, when the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole nations were relocated there under forced removal. Because the region was not yet a U.S. state, there are no ordinary birth, marriage or death certificates from this era; instead the key records are tribal enrollment rolls (such as the 1851 Old Settler Cherokee Roll and 1852 Drennen Roll), missionary church registers, and federal Indian-agency and land records, with digitized copies of several of these held free through FamilySearch and originals held by the National Archives. Several of the standard background guides this survey tried to check came back as generic, non-specific pages rather than Oklahoma-focused content, so some research-strategy details (and a full catalog of microfilm holdings) could not be confirmed and should be checked again directly on the FamilySearch Wiki or Catalog.

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to target specific ancestors against these tribal rolls and agency records.
