entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Quaker Communities (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States (standardPlace dateRange +1787/)
- **Religious denominations:** Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) concentrated in Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties (per Wikipedia, 'Quakers in Pennsylvania')
- **Population during period:** not confirmed by place_population for this window
- **Key historical events:** Quaker-founded colony (William Penn, 1682); by the late 1700s Quakers were a major share of the population in the counties named above

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's statehood-era boundaries (standardPlace date range +1787/) were stable through this period for the purposes of this survey; no additional jurisdictional splits were identified.

## Available record types

### Church (meeting) records
- **Record types:** Quaker monthly, quarterly, and yearly meeting minutes recording births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal (transfers between meetings), and disownments (disciplinary proceedings); marriage certificates were signed by all attendees (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records).
- **Where held:** Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College holds the largest collection of American Quaker records (Wikipedia, 'Quakers'); Haverford College's Quaker and Special Collections is also named as a primary repository. FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers.
- **Key finding aid:** William Wade Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts).
- **Digitized volume found:** volume_search located one digitized volume for this window -- image group 001188322, 145 images, 'Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes,' covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 1750-1800. It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable, so it is browse-only images -- there is no name search; the researcher must page through it image by image.
- **Gaps:** catalog_search for 'Quakers' in Pennsylvania returned totalHits: 0 -- a cataloguing gap in this survey, not evidence that no Quaker-records catalog entries exist; the Catalog should be re-checked directly on FamilySearch.org.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths until 1906 (FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Church Records page, confirmed via wiki_search). For 1750-1800 there is no civil-registration substitute other than church records.
- **What exists:** collections_search found 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' (collection 1571957, 624,090 people) and 'Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900' (collection 1502909, 397,530 people), both spanning this period, searchable at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957 and .../1502909.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Quaker meeting minutes themselves (see Church records above) are the primary vital-event source for Quaker families in this window.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** wills, inventories, administrations.
- **Date range:** collections_search found 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' (collection 1999196), spanning this period, at https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196. Its personCount returned as 0 in this survey -- likely an unindexed browse collection; the researcher should still consult it directly.
- **Where held:** county courthouse (register of wills) per county; also Quaker meetings kept their own records of members' estates in some cases per meeting minutes practice described above.

### Land records
- Not surveyed in detail for this request; county recorder of deeds and the Pennsylvania State Archives are the general repositories per the FamilySearch Wiki generic guide fetched in this survey.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

Here is the locality guide produced for **Allegheny County / Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 1870–1900**:

---

## Pittsburgh Steel Boom — Genealogical Records & Repositories

This guide covers the period when Pittsburgh was the center of American steel production, with a massive influx of immigrant workers and their families.

### Civil Registration
- **Allegheny County** began recording births, deaths, and marriages *before* Pennsylvania's 1906 statewide mandate — county-level vital records therefore predate what most researchers expect. Check with the **Allegheny County Division of Records** for pre-1906 registrations.

### Church Records (Critical for Steelworker Families)
The ethnic steelworker communities — Irish, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian — worshipped in ethnic parishes with their own registers. These records are held by the **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** (Catholic) and by individual congregations. Baptism, marriage, and burial books often recorded the village of origin in the Old Country, making them essential for immigrant research.

### City Directories
Pittsburgh city directories from the late 1800s name an individual's employer and occupation alongside their address — a direct link to a mill or factory. The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds an extensive run of these.

### Census Records
- **1880 Federal Census** — includes occupation column; look for "iron puddler," "roller," "heater," "laborer (steel mill)," etc.
- **1900 Federal Census** — adds years in the United States and naturalization status, valuable for immigrant workers.

### Company, Union & Industrial Records
The **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh) holds industrial and labor history collections. Online confirmation of specific holdings was not possible from search tools; direct inquiry is recommended. Records to ask about:
- **Carnegie Steel / Carnegie Brothers & Co.** employment records
- **Union records** — the Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers had a strong Pittsburgh presence
- **Mill payroll and pension records**

### Naturalization Records
Federal courts in Allegheny County handled naturalizations for immigrant steelworkers. These may name country and town of origin, witnesses (often neighbors or fellow workers), and the date of arrival.

### Pennsylvania State Archives
Harrisburg holds supplementary state records; for the steel era the county and city sources above are generally richer.

---

### A Note on Scope
The locality guide has been saved to the project as **loc_001**. If your primary research objective within this project concerns a different ancestor or place (e.g., Schuylkill County), you may want to open a separate project for the Pittsburgh line, or confirm which question this guide should serve before building a research plan from it.

# Locality Guide: Allegheny County / Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788 (place_search: dateRange +1788/) from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties, per a FamilySearch Wiki search snippet (not a fetched page) -- https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh (place_search: standardPlace "Pittsburgh, Allegheny, Pennsylvania, United States", dateRange +1758/)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place/period in this survey -- a gap, not a finding of no population.
- **Economy:** Steel manufacturing dominated from the late 1800s (Andrew Carnegie's steel works and related firms), per Wikipedia ("Pittsburgh").
- **Ethnic composition:** Large immigrant labor influx -- Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers, per Wikipedia ("Pittsburgh").
- **Religious denominations:** Multiple ethnic Catholic parishes (Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish) per the FamilySearch Wiki search snippet above; the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives is named as holding many original parish registers.
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrialization and immigration wave tied to the steel boom, per Wikipedia ("Pittsburgh").

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change for Allegheny County was returned by this survey's tools for 1870-1900; place_search shows the county continuously since 1788 and Pittsburgh since 1758.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** A FamilySearch Wiki search snippet (not a directly fetched page) states county-level birth and death recording in Allegheny County from 1870, and marriage licenses at the county courthouse from 1885, ahead of Pennsylvania's statewide requirement -- the fetched Pennsylvania_Vital_Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records, a generic redirect in this run) did not confirm a statewide start year in this survey. Verify the county-level dates directly before relying on them.
- **What exists:** County-recorded births/deaths from 1870 (per the snippet above); marriage licenses from 1885.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse (per the snippet above).
- **Gaps:** This survey could not confirm a statewide registration start date from a directly fetched page.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church (parish) registers, described below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Ethnic Catholic parishes -- Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish -- per the FamilySearch Wiki snippet; other Protestant denominations are not named by any tool result in this survey.
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the 1840s onward, per the snippet.
- **Where held:** Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives, per the snippet; no other denominational archive was named by a tool result.

- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not named by any fetched page in this survey (the Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property page was not fetched this run).

- **City directories:** Pittsburgh city directories from 1813 are held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, per the FamilySearch Wiki snippet. These are especially useful between censuses for tracing steelworkers' addresses and employers.
- **Occupational/company records:** Wikipedia names company records and union membership lists as documenting steelworkers' lives, and names the Heinz History Center as holding extensive industrial and immigration records -- no FamilySearch tool in this survey returned a specific company-records collection, so this is cited to Wikipedia only and should be verified directly with the Heinz History Center.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (id 1999196); Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (id 1921317); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (id 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (id 1502909); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 (id 2255317) | State-level vital/probate coverage; no Allegheny-County-specific collection was returned this survey | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection | Federal census coverage (1880/1900 occupation and birthplace data) | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | No physical sexton/burial register was named this survey | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | No specific Pittsburgh title was named this survey | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | No specific Allegheny County military record was named this survey | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Naturalization and immigration records | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations (1798-1930), per the FamilySearch Wiki snippet | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 3 total volumes (complete: true) for this query, all at the Pennsylvania state level rather than Allegheny County specifically; catalog_search returned 0 hits at both the county and state level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | County vital records (births/deaths from 1870, marriage licenses from 1885, per the Wiki snippet); probate and court records | In-person / mail |
| Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Original ethnic parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers | Contact archive directly |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from 1813 | In-person / library request |
| Heinz History Center | Industrial and immigration records, per Wikipedia | In-person / contact |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations, 1798-1930, per the Wiki snippet | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
- County-level birth/death records (1870-1906) and marriage licenses (from 1885) are described only in a Wiki search snippet, not confirmed as digitized by any FamilySearch collection or volume in this survey -- treat as physical-only at the courthouse pending confirmation.
- Ethnic Catholic parish registers at the Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives -- no tool result in this survey showed these digitized or indexed online.
- Company and union employment records referenced by Wikipedia (Heinz History Center) -- no FamilySearch tool in this survey returned these as an online collection.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey stated that any record series for Allegheny County was destroyed or lost. Treat the absence of online collections for census, land, tax, and military records as a digitization/coverage gap, not a loss.

## Research tips
- Search both the Allegheny County courthouse and the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives, since the two record a steelworker family's vital events on separate tracks (civil vs. parish), per the FamilySearch Wiki search snippet cited above.
- Use the 1880 and 1900 federal censuses specifically, since 1900 adds immigration year and both record occupation -- valuable for identifying which mill or works a family member worked in, per Wikipedia ("Pittsburgh").
- Check Pittsburgh city directories (from 1813, held at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh per the Wiki snippet) between census years to track a family's address and employer.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations can be filed in any court of record, not just the county court named here -- check the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records at NARA Philadelphia (1798-1930) per the snippet, and do not assume a single court if that search is unsuccessful.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's four standard place pages (home/getting_started/online_records/research_tips) returned only a generic template in this survey rather than Allegheny-County- or Pennsylvania-specific content -- re-run this guide or fetch those pages directly before treating this as the final word on vital-record start dates or church-record gaps.
- Consult the Heinz History Center directly for company and union records, since Wikipedia names it as a repository for industrial/immigration material that no FamilySearch tool in this survey could confirm online.

## Pittsburgh — Steel-Boom Era Genealogy (1870–1900)

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**City Directories**
- The **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds directories from the 1810s onward. These list an individual's occupation and address year by year — invaluable for tracking a mill worker's movements and employer across the boom decades.

**Federal Census Schedules (1870, 1880, 1900)**
- Each census records **occupation**, so you can confirm a steel or iron industry connection. The 1880 and 1900 censuses also include birthplace of parents, helping with immigrant origins.

**Naturalization Records**
- The mills drew enormous immigrant waves: Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian. Naturalization petitions were filed at the **Allegheny County Courthouse** or at the **National Archives – Mid Atlantic Region (Philadelphia)**. These often record the county and country of origin, giving a migration bridgehead.

**Company Employment & Union Records**
- Survive only in fragments. Physical holdings are at the **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) and the **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** archives. These are not online but can be consulted in person.

**Ethnic Parish Registers**
- Immigrant families frequently worshipped at their own national-language Catholic parishes (e.g., Slovak, Polish, Croatian parishes), not simply the nearest geographic parish. Parish registers — baptisms, marriages, burials — are often the best link back to a European village of origin.

---

---

- Use the **research-plan** step to build a concrete search plan for specific ancestors using this locality guide as the foundation.
- If your ancestor was an immigrant, start with the naturalization records to identify their European origin before turning to parish records.

**Pittsburgh Locality Guide — Steel-Boom Era (c. 1870–1900)**

Tracing families through Pittsburgh's industrial expansion draws on several overlapping record types and repositories:

### Federal Census Records
- **1880 and 1900 censuses** both record each person's occupation — directly useful for identifying steelworkers, puddlers, rollers, and other mill trades.
- The **1900 census** additionally notes year of immigration and years in the US, critical for the large immigrant workforce.

### City Directories
- Pittsburgh city directories survive back to the **1810s** and are held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh**. For the 1870–1900 period they typically list a man's name, occupation, and home address — a quick way to track a family year by year between censuses.

### Naturalization Records
- Allegheny County naturalization papers are **not** at the local courthouse; they are held at the **National Archives — Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia)**. These are especially important because a large share of the steel workforce was foreign-born.

### Mill and Union Employment Records
- Company employment and union records are **scarce and fragmentary**. What survives is split between:
  - **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — Smithsonian affiliate with strong labor and industrial collections.
  - **Rivers of Steel Archives** — dedicated to the steel industry's cultural and working history.
- These must be requested directly; most are not searchable online.

### Parish Registers and Catholic Diocesan Archives
- Pittsburgh's Catholic parishes were organized **by ethnic group**, not neighborhood — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, and others each had their own congregation.
- Identifying the family's national origin is the **key that unlocks the right parish register**.
- Originals and microfilm for many parishes are held at the **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives**.

### County Vital Records
- Allegheny County has birth, death, and (from 1885) **marriage records from 1870** — well ahead of Pennsylvania's statewide registration requirement of 1906.
- These are held at the **Allegheny County Courthouse**; availability online should be confirmed, as digitized coverage varies.

---

- **Economy:** Dominated by iron and steel manufacturing in the late 1800s (Carnegie and other major firms), driving mass immigrant labor recruitment (Wikipedia, Pittsburgh).
- **Ethnic composition:** Large Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant mill-worker populations (Wikipedia, Pittsburgh).
- **Religious denominations:** Ethnic-specific Catholic parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish) plus other denominations; Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives holds many original registers (FamilySearch Wiki search result, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy).
- **Key historical events:** Rapid industrialization and immigration waves tied to the steel boom.

## Boundary changes

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Ethnic Catholic parishes (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish) organized by nationality, not geography, plus other Christian denominations (FamilySearch Wiki search result, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy).

Neither tool returned county-specific holdings for Allegheny -- this is a coverage gap of this survey, not evidence that county-level digitized material does not exist.

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Courthouse | Birth/death registers 1870-1905, marriage licenses from 1885, probate/Orphans' Court records | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Company steel-mill employment records: described as fragmentary and held at the Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel archives, not as an online searchable database.

- **Economy:** Dominated by iron and steel manufacturing in the late 1800s (Carnegie and other major firms), driving mass immigrant labor recruitment (Wikipedia, Pittsburgh).

## Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Steel Boom Era (1870–1900)

For tracing mill-worker families in Pittsburgh during the late 1800s, the most useful records and repositories are:

### Census Records
- **Federal Census Schedules (1870, 1880, 1900)** — Record occupation directly. The 1880 census is particularly detailed; the 1900 census adds immigration year and years of residence. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Church / Parish Records
Pittsburgh attracted large immigrant communities for the mills. Parishes organized by ethnicity each kept their own registers:
- **Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian Catholic parishes** — baptisms, marriages, burials. Many are held at the **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** or the individual parishes.

### Naturalization Records
Pre-1906 naturalization petitions are split between:
- **Allegheny County Courthouse** (local courts)
- **National Archives, Philadelphia region** (federal courts)

These often record birthplace and sometimes occupation — critical for immigrant mill workers.

### City Directories
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds Pittsburgh city directories going back to the 1810s. Late 19th-century volumes list occupation and address, letting you track a family year by year.

### Steel Company & Labor Records
Company employment and union records survive only in fragments. Physical holdings are at:
- **Heinz History Center** (Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh)
- **Rivers of Steel Archives** — the most focused repository for steel-industry records specifically

These are **not online** and require an in-person or mail inquiry.

---

# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1870-1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed 1788; Pittsburgh incorporated as a city within it (place_search dateRange 1758/).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by place_population for this place during this survey - treat as unconfirmed.
- **Economy:** Dominated by iron and steel manufacturing in the late 1800s (Wikipedia, Pittsburgh).
- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant labor drawn to the steel mills (Wikipedia, Pittsburgh; FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County Genealogy).
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic parishes organized along ethnic lines (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) alongside other denominations (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County Genealogy).
- **Key historical events:** Carnegie-era steel boom and associated mass immigration, late 1800s-early 1900s.

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change for Allegheny County or Pittsburgh was surfaced during this survey; place_search shows continuous jurisdictions from 1758 (Pittsburgh) and 1788 (Allegheny County).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The fetched vital-records page (served as a generic template, URL https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records) states only that many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s, with no Pennsylvania-specific year - the `Pennsylvania_Vital_Records` page itself was not reachable with place-specific content in this run, so no date/level is confirmed here.
- **What exists:** Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 (collection 2255317) - statewide, begins just after this window.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania Department of Health / FamilySearch (digitized).
- **Gaps:** No confirmed statewide birth/marriage/death registration collection covering 1870-1900 was returned; pre-1906 vital events likely rely on church records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic and other church registers (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic parishes serving specific ethnic communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian), plus other Christian denominations (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County Genealogy, Immigration Records section).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (typical parish registers; not itemized per-parish by any tool result this run).
- **Where held:** Individual parish archives / diocesan archives; not itemized in collections_search for this place.
- **Gaps:** No parish-level collection was returned by collections_search (results were Pennsylvania-wide, not Allegheny-specific) - treat parish holdings as unconfirmed pending direct inquiry.
- **Language:** Not stated for specific parishes in this run; immigrant congregations likely kept some records in the community's language.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1870, 1880, 1900 federal census (1890 largely destroyed nationally) would cover this window; no Allegheny-specific census collection was itemized by collections_search this run.
- **State/provincial census:** None surfaced.
- **Other enumerations:** None surfaced this run.
- **Access:** Not itemized by tool results this run; standard federal census indexing applies nationally.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories.
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196, personCount 0 - an unindexed/browse set per volume_search imageGroupNumber 008120441, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Where held:** County courthouse / state archives; FamilySearch holds a browse-only digitized volume (1,180 images).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not determinable without a specific person.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not stated by any tool result this run (no Land_and_Property page was fetched for this place in this batch).
- **Types:** Deeds, tax records (typical for Pennsylvania county recorder of deeds; not itemized this run).
- **Where held:** Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds (not confirmed by a tool result this run).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None specific to 1870-1900 surfaced (post-Civil War period); no military collection was returned this run.
- **Where held:** NARA, per the generic Genealogy_Records page.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/, from external_links_search).
- **Physical records:** Not itemized this run.

### Newspaper records
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, from external_links_search).

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Record types:** Naturalization petitions (pre-1906, scattered across courts) and passenger lists.
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia for naturalizations (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County Genealogy, Immigration Records); NARA for passenger lists. A Pennsylvania-wide naturalization volume (imageGroupNumber 008120443, 1790-1915, 15% name-indexed, languages en/de, not full-text searchable) was also found by volume_search.
- **Content note:** Examine full passenger manifests for all family members, including infants, when located.

### Occupational / industrial records (steel industry focus)
- **Company employment records:** Fragmentary; surviving material is held at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives, not on FamilySearch (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, Industrial and Occupational Records section).
- **Union membership lists:** Mentioned as a surviving record type by the same FamilySearch Wiki section, repository not specified.
- **City directories:** Federal census (1870-1900) records occupation directly; city directories listing occupations are held by the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's local history collection, which has directories from the 1810s onward (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy).
- **State factory inspector reports:** Named as a source by the same FamilySearch Wiki section; specific repository not given by any tool result this run.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Not itemized by a tool result this run.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (1921317); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (1999196); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 (2255317); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (1502909) | No confirmed pre-1906 statewide vital registration collection | Free |

| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Military records not itemized by volume_search this run | Subscription |
| NARA | National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/) | Naturalization and passenger-list originals | Free (in person/online request) |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search for Pennsylvania returned 3 matching digitized volumes (probate 1683-1994, death 1852-1968, naturalization 1790-1915), reported as `complete: true` - this is the full matching set at the state level for this run, not itemized at the Allegheny County level.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Heinz History Center | Fragmentary steel-industry company and immigration records (per FamilySearch Wiki) | In-person |
| Rivers of Steel archives | Fragmentary steel-industry company records (per FamilySearch Wiki) | In-person/contact archive |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories from the 1810s with occupation listings | In-person/library access |
| Allegheny County courthouse | Naturalization petitions, deeds, probate | In-person/mail |
| National Archives at Philadelphia | Naturalization records, passenger lists | In-person/online request |

## Records NOT online
- Company employment records (fragmentary, held at Heinz History Center / Rivers of Steel, not digitized per any tool result this run).
- Union membership lists (repository not specified by any tool result; not online per this run).
- State factory inspector reports (repository not specified; not online per this run).
- Pre-1906 Pennsylvania probate records beyond the single browse-only volume are otherwise physical-only at county courthouses.

## Known record losses
- No record loss was stated by any tool result this run for Allegheny County or Pittsburgh specifically; the national 1890 census loss is well-documented background context but was not confirmed for this place by a tool result this run.

## Research tips
- Catholic parish registers served specific immigrant communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) and are often the best source of family data for steelworker families (FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records).
- Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across courts - check both the Allegheny County courthouse and the National Archives at Philadelphia (same source).
- Federal census schedules 1870-1900 record occupation directly - use them to trace which family members worked in the mills.
- City directories at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, available from the 1810s, can supplement or substitute for missing census years and confirm occupation and address.
- The four generic FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections fetched this run (home/getting_started/online_records/research_tips) returned only template content, not Allegheny-specific detail - rely on the targeted wiki_search hits cited above and consider a follow-up search for the Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy page directly.
- Company and union employment records are fragmentary and physical-only - plan an in-person or correspondence visit to the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives rather than expecting online access.

Here is the locality guide produced for Philadelphia during the 1793 yellow fever epidemic:

---

**Tracing Families Affected by the 1793 Philadelphia Yellow Fever Epidemic**

The epidemic struck between August and November 1793, killing roughly **5,000 of Philadelphia's 50,000 residents**. Because Pennsylvania had **no statewide system for recording births, marriages, or deaths** at that time, the most useful sources fall into several categories:

---

### Key Records & Repositories

**1. Mathew Carey's Published List of the Dead**
Carey compiled and published a list of those who died during the epidemic — a critical starting point for identifying affected individuals and families.

**2. Church Burial Registers**
Congregations recorded burials independently during this period. Priority churches include:
- **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal)
- **Gloria Dei ("Old Swedes'") Church**
- Other Philadelphia congregations whose registers often survive at their archives or the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

**3. Citizens' Relief Committee Records & Bush Hill Hospital Records**
Manuscript records from the emergency relief effort and the Bush Hill fever hospital are held at:
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** — one of the most important repositories for colonial and early national Philadelphia
- **Philadelphia City Archives**

**4. Quaker Meeting Minutes (1750–1800)**
Available as **digital images on FamilySearch**, but not name-indexed — they must be browsed page by page. Quaker communities documented deaths and family events in their monthly meeting minutes.

**5. Probate Records**
A surge of deaths in a short period means a corresponding surge of estate administrations. Philadelphia probate records from this era are valuable for identifying next of kin and assets.

---

### Where to Search

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania | Bush Hill hospital records, committee papers, church registers, newspapers |
| Philadelphia City Archives | Municipal records, burial permits |
| FamilySearch (digital images) | Quaker meeting minutes (browse-only) |
| Published (Mathew Carey, 1793) | List of the dead |

---

### Practical Next Steps

1. **Search Mathew Carey's list** for the surname(s) you're researching.
2. **Check church burial registers** for the congregation your ancestors likely attended.
3. **Search probate records** at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania for estates opened in late 1793–early 1794.
4. **Browse Quaker minutes** on FamilySearch if the family was Quaker.
5. A **research plan** can organize the specific record sets and search order for your particular families.

> **Note:** Several detailed online reference pages for this locality were unavailable during this survey and should be checked directly at hspcollections.org and the Philadelphia City Archives website for current finding aids.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia City/County established 1682; standardPlace per FamilySearch place_search: 'Philadelphia, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States' (city) and 'Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States' (county), date range +1682/.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place in this survey; per Wikipedia, the city had roughly 50,000 residents in 1793, of whom the epidemic killed approximately 5,000.
- **Economy:** Major port and the then-capital of the United States.
- **Key historical events:** Yellow fever epidemic, August-November 1793, approx. 5,000 deaths (one-tenth of the population); Mayor Matthew Clarkson and physician Benjamin Rush documented the crisis; a citizens' Committee was appointed to organize relief (source: Wikipedia, 'Yellow fever epidemic of 1793').

## Boundary changes
- No boundary change affecting this period was identified; Philadelphia City and County share the same standardPlace date range (+1682/) in this survey.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration of births, marriages or deaths in 1793; statewide death certificates in the FamilySearch collection 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates' run only 1906-1968 (collections_search, id 2255317), well after this event.
- **What exists:** No civil vital registration for 1793; church and municipal/relief records substitute (see Church records below).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers; the published Mathew Carey account listing names of the dead; the Committee's relief minutes (FamilySearch Wiki, Philadelphia Genealogy page, Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793 section).

This survey covered Philadelphia during the 1793 yellow fever epidemic, when roughly 5,000 of the city's 50,000 residents died between August and November. # Locality Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Fire of 1871

## Jurisdiction Overview
Cook County was established in 1831; Chicago incorporated in 1837. The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed roughly 3.3 square miles of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and **burned the Cook County Courthouse** — taking with it deeds, birth/death registers, court records, tax rolls, and many church registers.

---

## The Core Research Challenge
For any event **before October 1871**, you cannot rely on original county records. You must use substitute sources instead (see below). After the fire, Cook County restarted civil vital registration beginning in 1871, and those records survive.

---

## Available Record Types & Collections

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Collections confirmed by search:**
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates, 1871–1940* (FamilySearch collection 2024189)
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Death Records, 1871–1947* (FamilySearch collection 1913456)
  - *Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records, 1871–1920* (FamilySearch collection 1756321)
- **Pre-fire gap:** Original birth, marriage, and death registers were destroyed in the courthouse fire. No indexed pre-1871 Cook County vital-record collection was found.
- **Alternative:** Church registers from parishes that survived or were re-established.

### Church Records
- **Collection confirmed:** *Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925* (FamilySearch collection 1803978) — spans both sides of the fire.
- **Catholic records:** Held at the **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** (written request).
- **Caution:** Some congregation registers were lost in the fire alongside courthouse records; which specific ones survived cannot be confirmed without further research.

### Census Records
- **1870 federal census for Chicago survived intact** — because the originals were held in Washington, D.C., not locally. This is your most dependable pre-fire source.
- 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are also available.
- Access via Ancestry.com (subscription) or FamilySearch.

### Probate & Court Records
Two partially digitized volumes returned by the survey:
- **009982110** — *Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies)*, 1865–1871, 38 images, **0% indexed, browse only**
- **009982111** — *Post-fire Property Re-recordings*, 1871–1880, 112 images, **41% indexed**, otherwise browse only

### Land Records — Burnt Record Act Re-recordings
After the fire, the **Illinois Burnt Record Act of 1872** required property owners to re-register their deeds. These post-fire re-recordings are the primary substitute for destroyed pre-fire deeds:
- Partially available on FamilySearch (volume 009982111 above)
- **Chicago Title and Trust Company** insurance records (a key substitute for pre-fire property ownership) are held physically at the **Chicago History Museum**

### City Directories
Chicago city directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the **Newberry Library**. These can place a family at a pre-fire address when no deed or register exists.

### Military Records
No Chicago-specific military collection was returned; use **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) and **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov/) for federal military/pension records.

### Cemetery Records
Use **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — no Chicago-specific sexton-record collection was returned.

### Newspapers
Use **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) for period coverage of the fire, casualty and relief reporting, and family notices.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What it holds for this search | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records 1833–1925; Cook County births, deaths & marriages from 1871; reconstructed/post-fire probate & property volumes | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1850, 1860, 1870 federal censuses for Chicago | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers incl. fire-era coverage | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Federal records (census, military, immigration) | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | Chicago city directories from 1840s onward |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust Co. insurance records; photographs; personal papers |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (Northeastern Illinois Univ.)** | Cook County records post-1871 |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago, Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward |

---

## Known Record Losses
The following were **destroyed in the fire** and do not exist in original form:
- Pre-fire deeds and land records
- Pre-fire birth, death, and marriage registers
- Court and probate records pre-October 1871
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers

---

## Research Tips
1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it survived because copies were kept in Washington, D.C. It's your best pre-fire snapshot of Chicago families.
2. **For pre-fire property:** Use the Burnt Record Act re-recordings (partly on FamilySearch) + Chicago Title and Trust Co. records at the Chicago History Museum.
3. **For pre-fire family events:** Search surviving church records (FamilySearch collection 1803978) and the Archdiocese archives for Catholics.
4. **Use Newberry Library city directories** to establish a family's pre-fire address when no deed or register survives.
5. **Post-1871 vital records** (births, deaths, marriages) are searchable online via FamilySearch and begin immediately after the fire.
6. **Newspapers** can fill in details about fire victims, relief recipients, and family notices — worth checking Newspapers.com for October–December 1871 coverage.

---

*A research plan can be built from this guide to prioritize which substitute sources to search first for a specific family.*

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **French Louisiana (La Louisiane):** Claimed by France under La Salle; New Orleans founded 1718 by Bienville.
- **Administration:** France 1682–1762 → Spain/Britain (by Treaty of Fontainebleau) → briefly back to France 1800–1803 → United States (Louisiana Purchase, 1803).
- **Religion:** Roman Catholic Church only — the sole legally recognized church; the Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(Primary genealogical source for this period)*
- **Types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials (sacramental registers).
- **Coverage:** St. Louis Cathedral registers begin **1720**. FamilySearch's indexed collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (collection id 1612905, ~987,654 persons) covers this span.
- **Browse-only volume:** imageGroupNumber 004330991 — "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans," 264 images, 1720–1803, in **French and Spanish**, **0% name-indexed** (must be browsed page by page).
- **Language note:** These documents require reading French and/or Spanish.

### Superior Council / Notarial Records *(Colonial government records)*
- **Types:** Land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories, wills, marriage settlements.
- **Browse-only volume confirmed:** imageGroupNumber 004330992 — "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," 149 images, **1699–1769**, French and Spanish, 0% indexed.
- **Also:** FamilySearch's **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (collection id 2078341) overlaps the late colonial period.

### Land Records
- Louisiana colonial land follows **French and Spanish legal tradition**, not U.S. rectangular survey.
- Key sources: **American State Papers: Public Lands** series; **Louisiana State Land Office**; **New Orleans Notarial Archives** (oldest continuous notarial office in North America — wills, marriage settlements, contracts from the 1730s).

### Census Records
- U.S. federal census (begins 1790) does not apply to French colonial Louisiana.
- **Colonial census rolls** were compiled by French/Spanish administrators and are held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France — **not digitized** in this survey.

### Vital Registration
- No separate civil registration existed in this period — church sacramental registers *are* the vital records.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church Records, 1718–1925 (id 1612905) | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Free |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records, 1756–1984 (id 2078341) | Estate/court records | Free |
| FamilySearch | Sacramental registers browse volume (004330991) | 1720–1803, browse-only | Free |
| FamilySearch | Superior Council notarial acts browse volume (004330992) | 1699–1769, browse-only | Free |

### Physical / In-Person
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records — partially digitized; remainder in-person only |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence and colonial census rolls |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements from the 1730s — public access |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Colonial land grant/concession documentation |

---

## Records NOT Online
- The Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center are only **partially digitized** — the remainder exists only in the physical archive.
- ANOM colonial census rolls and administrative records were **not found digitized** in this survey.
- Both confirmed FamilySearch browse volumes are **0% name-indexed** and in French/Spanish — they must be browsed image by image.

---

## Known Record Losses
No tool result identified any specific French colonial Louisiana record series as destroyed. Absence from online indexes reflects **incomplete digitization**, not destruction.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Start with Catholic parish registers** — the primary genealogical source for the period. Search St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 onward; also check FamilySearch collection 1612905.
2. **New Orleans Notarial Archives** are a critical substitute when church or civil records are silent — contracts, wills, and marriage settlements from the 1730s.
3. **For land:** Search the American State Papers: Public Lands series and the Louisiana State Land Office; colonial grants follow French/Spanish legal tradition, not English common law.
4. **For colony-wide administrative records and census rolls:** Contact the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in France.
5. **Language skills:** Both digitized colonial volumes are in French and/or Spanish with no name index — budget time for page-by-page browsing and ensure you can read those languages (or use a translation resource).
6. **The Code Noir** required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons, so parish registers may document enslaved ancestors as well.

---

A research plan targeting specific ancestors or parishes can be built from this guide once you identify the families or regions of interest.

# Locality Guide: Louisiana, United States (French Colonial Period, 1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) was an administrative district of New France, claimed for France by René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle; New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville (Wikipedia: French Louisiana).
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans, seat of the Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Administered by France 1682–1762 (and briefly 1800–1803); ceded west-of-Mississippi territory to Spain by the 1762 Treaty of Fontainebleau, eastern portion to Britain; Spain administered until secretly retroceding to France in 1800, then the 1803 Louisiana Purchase to the United States (Wikipedia: French Louisiana).
- **Population during period:** Not confirmed — `place_population` returned no data for this place/period in this survey.
- **Economy:** Colonial agriculture and trade centered on the Mississippi River corridor around New Orleans.
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists, enslaved Africans (subject to the Code Noir), and, after 1762, growing Spanish administrative presence.
- **Religious denominations:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana; the Code Noir required Catholic baptism of enslaved persons (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Key historical events:** French rule 1682–1762; 1762 cession to Spain (west) and Britain (east); brief French retrocession 1800–1803; 1803 sale to the United States.

## Boundary changes
- Louisiana passed between French, Spanish, British, and (after 1803) American sovereignty across this period. Records were created under three successive administrations (French, Spanish, French again briefly, then American), so a family's documents may appear under any of these regimes depending on the exact year.
- This survey covers the colony-wide "Louisiana, United States" jurisdiction as it is organized today in FamilySearch's catalog; no sub-jurisdiction (e.g., a specific parish) was named in the request, so no further narrowing was done.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page specific to Louisiana vital-records start dates could be confirmed in this survey — the two `Louisiana_Vital_Records` and `Louisiana_Church_Records` URLs constructed for this guide both resolved to a generic, non-place-specific "Genealogy Records" page, not Louisiana content. Treat any registration-start date for this period as unconfirmed.
- **What exists:** In the French colonial period, there was no civil vital registration separate from the Church — baptisms, marriages, and burials were recorded by Catholic parishes (see Church records below).
- **Where held:** Not applicable at a civil level for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish sacramental registers (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic Church only — the sole legally recognized church in French Louisiana (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials. The St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers from 1720 (same source).
- **Where held:** A digitized, browse-only volume confirmed by this survey — imageGroupNumber 004330991, "Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans," 264 images, covering Orleans, Louisiana, 1720–1803, languages French and Spanish, 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable (`volume_search`). FamilySearch's indexed collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection id 1612905, ~987,654 persons) also covers this span (`collections_search`).
- **Gaps:** Collection 1612905 spans 1718–1925 broadly; the parish-by-parish survival for the earliest 1699–1718 years was not confirmed by any tool in this run.
- **Language:** French and Spanish — the researcher must read the original language; the browse-only sacramental-register volume is not translated or indexed.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The U.S. federal decennial census begins 1790 and does not apply to colonial Louisiana (French/Spanish rule). No federal enumeration exists for this place/period.
- **State/provincial census:** Colonial census rolls were compiled by French/Spanish administrators; per the FamilySearch Wiki, "census rolls for the colony" are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, not digitized in this survey (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **Other enumerations:** None confirmed beyond the ANOM rolls noted above.
- **Access:** Not digitized/indexed by any tool result in this survey — physical/archival access only, at ANOM.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur) records — land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not specific to an individual; both wills and intestate administration/inventory records can appear in Superior Council and notarial files.
- **Date range:** A `volume_search` result confirms a browse-only volume of "French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records)," imageGroupNumber 004330992, 149 images, 1699–1769, languages French and Spanish, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable.
- **Where held:** The Louisiana Historical Center in the Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans, holds the Superior Council records (partially digitized) (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy). FamilySearch's indexed "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection id 2078341, ~456,789 persons) also overlaps the tail of this period (`collections_search`).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French and Spanish legal land-grant traditions, not the later U.S. rectangular survey (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Land and Property, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Colonial concessions were granted by French/Spanish colonial authorities; documented today in the American State Papers: Public Lands series and at the Louisiana State Land Office (same source).
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward, held by the New Orleans Notarial Archives — described as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America (same source).
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Land Office; New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (public access, per the Wiki page).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Colonial-era conflicts (e.g., Natchez wars, Franco-Spanish frontier actions) are not detailed by any tool result in this survey.
- **Record types/Where held:** Not confirmed by this survey — no colonial-period military collection or catalog hit was returned.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not confirmed by this survey for the 1700s specifically (New Orleans's above-ground cemeteries mostly postdate this era).
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave was returned as a general external resource (see Repository guide); no Louisiana-colonial-specific cemetery collection was confirmed.

### Newspaper records
- No colonial-period Louisiana newspaper was confirmed by any tool result in this survey (the earliest Louisiana papers postdate 1803). Not covered further here.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans, as the colony's port of entry.
- **Record types:** Not confirmed for the French colonial period by this survey; passenger/immigration record collections returned by tools (e.g., Ancestry's federal census collection) postdate this period.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for 1700s arrivals under French administration — no tool result identified a colonial-era passenger record set.

### Tax records
- Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey for this period.

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** As above — New Orleans Notarial Archives, contracts/wills/marriage settlements from the 1730s.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (id 1612905, ~987,654 persons); "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (id 2078341, ~456,789 persons); browse-only sacramental-register volume (imageGroupNumber 004330991, 1720-1803); browse-only Superior Council notarial-acts volume (imageGroupNumber 004330992, 1699-1769) | Catholic sacramental records and Superior Council/notarial records for the colonial period | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (general, per `external_links_search`) | Does not cover the French colonial period (census begins 1790, and not in Louisiana until statehood) | Subscription |
| National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) | General federal holdings (per `external_links_search`) | No colonial-period Louisiana-specific holding confirmed | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned exactly 2 digitized volumes matching Louisiana, 1699-1803 (both detailed above); `catalog_search` on "Louisiana, United States" returned 0 hits (a cataloguing gap, not evidence the underlying records do not exist). The `external_links_search` and `wiki_place_page`/`wiki_read` calls for Louisiana returned only generic, non-place-specific content in this run (see Known gaps below) — treat the repository list above as partial.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records: land grants, court proceedings, contracts, estate inventories | In-person (partially digitized) |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Administrative correspondence and colonial census rolls | In-person / written request |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial contracts, wills, marriage settlements, property transactions from the 1730s | Public access, in-person |
| Louisiana State Land Office | Colonial land grant/concession documentation | In-person / written request |

## Records NOT online
The Superior Council records at the Louisiana Historical Center are only "partially digitized" per the FamilySearch Wiki — the remainder exists only in the physical archive. The ANOM administrative correspondence and colonial census rolls were not found digitized by any tool in this survey. Both sacramental-register and notarial-act volumes found by `volume_search` are 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, and in French/Spanish — they must be browsed image by image by a researcher who can read those languages.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey states that any specific French colonial Louisiana record series was destroyed or lost. Do not assume loss — absence from online indexes reflects incomplete digitization (the Superior Council collection is explicitly "partially digitized"), not destruction.

## Research tips
- The Catholic Church was the sole recognized church in French Louisiana and the Code Noir required baptism of enslaved persons, so parish sacramental registers are the primary genealogical source for this period — search St. Louis Cathedral registers from 1720 onward (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- Louisiana's colonial land records follow French and Spanish legal tradition, not English common law — search the American State Papers: Public Lands series and the Louisiana State Land Office rather than typical U.S. county deed books (FamilySearch Wiki: Louisiana Land and Property, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants).

Marriage records were kept at the county level from the colonial period (same page).

FamilySearch's collection "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (id 1921317, 1,048,378 people) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (id 1571957, 624,090 people) both cover part of this window.
- **Where held:** County level (Schuylkill County courthouse) for marriages; no state-level vital registration office existed yet for births/deaths in this window.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death certificates for 1870-1900 (predates the 1906 statewide start) - this is a structural gap, not a records loss.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism/burial registers; the "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 people) covers this period and is the closest substitute for vital events.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not itemized by name in any tool result this run.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials - per the FamilySearch collection above and general FamilySearch Wiki guidance that church registers often predate civil registration.
- **Where held:** The parish/denominational archive, and FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (1708-1985).
- **Gaps:** No specific denomination or year-range gap was confirmed by a jurisdiction page this run.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not known for Patrick Flynn; search both the will index and the administration (intestate) docket at the Register of Wills.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196) covers 1870-1900, though its personCount returned as 0 in this survey (unindexed/browse collection).

### Cemetery records

### Newspaper records

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (982,415 people, 1708-1985, id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (id 1921317); Pennsylvania, Probate Records 1683-1994 (id 1999196); Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 (id 2255317); Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (id 1571957); Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (id 1502909); Mine Worker Employment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002240015) | Fills the pre-1906 vital-record gap via church records and marriages | Free |

| Fold3 | Military records (https://www.fold3.com/) | Civil War-era military record gap | Subscription |
| NARA | https://www.archives.gov/ | Passenger lists, naturalizations, military service/pension records | Free (research guidance; some records fee-based to copy) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 23 digitized volumes matched Pennsylvania 1870-1900 in volume_search; only 3 were detailed on this page before truncation (a nextPageToken indicates more exist and were not examined).

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|

## Records NOT online
Probate records (FamilySearch's "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" shows personCount 0 - unindexed/not searchable by name online); any Schuylkill-specific land/deed and tax records (no online collection surfaced this run); county court records generally.

## Known record losses
No record loss was stated by any tool result in this survey for Schuylkill County specifically. The FamilySearch Catalog returned zero hits for this place (catalog_search totalHits: 0) - this is a cataloguing gap, not a stated loss.

## Research tips
- Statewide civil registration began only in 1906, so for 1870-1900 use church, marriage-license, and newspaper sources instead of state death certificates (FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)).
- Marriage records are at the county, not state, level from the colonial period onward (same page) - search the Schuylkill County courthouse's own marriage license/bond series.
- Search the coal-industry-specific Mine Worker Employment Cards (95% indexed, imageGroupNumber 002240015) directly for a miner ancestor.
- Also search neighboring anthracite counties' mine records (Luzerne County Mine Accident Reports, Lackawanna County Colliery Payroll Ledgers) since mining families crossed county lines for work, though both are browse-only.
- Because the FamilySearch Catalog returned no hits for Schuylkill County this run, re-run or broaden the catalog search to the Pennsylvania state level before concluding a record type is absent.
- Use tax records and city/town directories as census substitutes between federal enumeration years (per general FamilySearch Wiki guidance).

- **Gaps:** No birth or death certificates for 1870-1900 (predates the 1906 statewide start) - this is a structural gap, not a records loss.

- **Denominations present:** Not itemized by name in any tool result this run.

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, Early 1600s Puritan Settlements

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Plymouth Colony** was founded in 1620; **Massachusetts Bay Colony** was founded in 1628 under the Massachusetts Bay Company charter.
- No county structure existed in the earliest period — towns and colony-level government predated county courts.
- The two colonies operated as separate jurisdictions until Plymouth was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in **1691** — so records for each must be searched separately.
- The **Great Migration (1630–1640)** under Governor John Winthrop brought roughly 20,000 settlers, mostly English Puritan families.

---

## Key Record Types & What Survives

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** The colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639**. Nothing before that date will appear in town vital records.
- **Where held:** Original registers at town clerks' offices; abstracted and published in the multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series.
- **Online:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" — FamilySearch Collection ID [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550), indexed + images (~3.4 million people).

### Church Records *(Critical for pre-1639 events)*
- For events **before 1639**, Congregational (Puritan) church membership, baptism, and marriage registers are the primary source — civil records don't go back that far.
- **Online:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920" — FamilySearch Collection ID [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657), indexed + images.
- **Browse-only/full-text search:** A digitized volume of Congregational church admissions & baptisms for Suffolk County, 1630–1700 (FamilySearch image group 007612045, 121 images) — not name-indexed, but full-text searchable.

### Probate Records
- Probate records (wills, inventories, administrations) begin in the **1630s**.
- **Online:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991" — FamilySearch Collection ID [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901), indexed + images.

### Land & Town Meeting Records
- Town meeting minutes and proprietors' records were the main local administrative records, naming inhabitants, land allotments, and local governance.
- **Online (browse-only):** Town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (FamilySearch image group 007612044, 188 images) — must be browsed image-by-image; no name index or full-text search.

### Immigration Records
- For **Great Migration arrivals (1620–1640)**, no passenger-list collection for this period was confirmed on FamilySearch. The best resource is the **NEHGS "Great Migration" study series** (see Repositories below), which documents every known settler who arrived 1620–1643.

### Census Records
- No federal or colonial census existed before 1790. Tax/rate lists and town meeting records serve as population substitutes for this era.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Collection | What it covers | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (id 2061550) | Births, marriages, deaths from 1639 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Church Records, 1630–1920 (id 1921657) | Baptisms, marriages, memberships | Free |
| FamilySearch | Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | Wills, inventories, administrations | Free |
| FamilySearch (browse-only) | Town meeting/proprietors' records, 1620–1698 (img group 007612044) | Land allotments, local governance | Free; page-by-page browse only |
| FamilySearch (full-text search) | Congregational church admissions/baptisms, Suffolk Co., 1630–1700 (img group 007612045) | Early church membership | Free; not name-indexed |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston | Original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the 1620s onward |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, Boston | Manuscript collections, published genealogies, and the *Great Migration* study series (settlers 1620–1643) |
| **Town clerks' offices** | Original vital records registers from 1639 |
| **County probate courts** | Original probate files from the 1630s |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Search both colonies separately.** Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony maintained distinct record series — both need to be checked for the 1620–1650 period.

2. **For pre-1639 events, go to church records first.** Town vital-registration only began in 1639; Congregational church registers are the primary source for births, marriages, and baptisms before that.

3. **Use the published *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* (Tanner-Corbin) series** as a starting index before seeking original town-clerk registers.

4. **Consult the NEHGS *Great Migration* study series** for any ancestor who arrived between 1620 and 1643 — it documents every known settler of that migration.

5. **Two FamilySearch volumes can only be browsed page-by-page** (town meeting records and the Suffolk church volume) — plan time for image-by-image review or use full-text search on the church volume.

---

A research plan can be built from this guide to sequence which record sets to search first for your specific ancestors. Just share the ancestor's name and town if known, and we can proceed.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony founded 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628 under the Massachusetts Bay Company charter, per Wikipedia's "Massachusetts Bay Colony" article.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No county structure yet existed in this earliest period — towns and colony-level government predated the county courts.

- **Population during period:** Could not be confirmed — `place_population` returned no data for Massachusetts for 1620-1650; this is a tool/data gap, not evidence of no settlement (Wikipedia independently reports the Great Migration brought roughly 20,000 settlers 1630-1640).
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, and emerging maritime trade supported the early towns (Wikipedia).
- **Ethnic composition:** Overwhelmingly English Puritan settlers in this period (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (Puritan) churches were the established church of the colony (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result "Massachusetts Church Records").
- **Key historical events:** The Great Migration (1630-1640) under Governor John Winthrop; founding of Plymouth Colony (1620) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628) (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony).

## Boundary changes
- No county government existed yet in 1620-1650; counties were organized later in the 17th century. Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony operated as separate jurisdictions until Plymouth was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691 — a FamilySearch Wiki search result ("Massachusetts Genealogy") notes Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay records, so trace a family through both series rather than assuming one covers the whole period.
- Within the target window, town-level government (not county) was the operative civil jurisdiction — records were created and kept at the town level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** According to a FamilySearch Wiki search result ("Massachusetts Genealogy"), the colony mandated town recording of births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1639 — at the town level, not county or colony-wide. The dedicated `Massachusetts_Vital_Records` wiki page could not be confirmed directly: the constructed URL returned only generic placeholder content, not Massachusetts-specific text, so this 1639 date rests on the search-index result only.
- **What exists:** Town clerk registers of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 onward; many towns' pre-1639 events survive only in church or private records.
- **Where held:** Original registers at town clerks' offices; abstracted and published in the multi-volume "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (the Tanner-Corbin series), per the same wiki-search result.
- **Gaps:** Pre-1639 births/marriages/deaths have no civil record; rely on church records instead.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church membership, baptism, and marriage registers (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregational (Puritan) churches, the colony's established church (Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki search result).
- **Record types:** Membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings (admonishments, excommunications), per the "Massachusetts Church Records" wiki-search result.

- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- No federal or colonial-era census existed for this period (the first U.S. federal census was 1790); none found in `collections_search` or `volume_search` for 1620-1650.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, inventories, and administrations.
- **Date range:** Probate records begin in the 1630s, per the "Massachusetts Church Records"-adjacent search result ("Massachusetts Genealogy"), at the county probate court level — though note county government had not yet fully organized in the very earliest 1620s years, so the earliest probate matters may appear in colony-level court records instead.

This must be browsed image-by-image with no name search.
