# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States — Land Run Era (1889–1907)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Oklahoma Territory** was organized in 1890 from land opened by the Land Run of April 22, 1889. It merged with Indian Territory in 1907 to form the State of Oklahoma.
- **Capital during territorial years:** Guthrie.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States federal territory (prior to 1907 statehood).
- **Key context:** Many Land Run settlers arrived from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. Tracing families before 1889 often requires searching departure-state records.

---

## Most Important Record Types

### 🏡 Land Records (Central to This Period)
- **Record types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, and *rejected* applications (rejected claims still contain family detail — don't skip them).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (234,567 people).
- **Digitized volume:** Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, Oklahoma 1889–1907 — 74% name-indexed, with images.
- **Where held:** National Archives (Record Group 49, General Land Office); also searchable free at **BLM's General Land Office Records** site (glorecords.blm.gov).
- **Why important:** Homestead final proofs include witness statements and proof of settlement — they often substitute for missing vital or court records.

### 📋 Census Records
- **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census:** One of the few surviving 1890 census records in the nation (most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed). Held by the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.
- **Regular federal decennial censuses** also cover the territory.

### ⚖️ Territorial District Court Records (1890–1907)
- Covers civil, criminal, **probate**, and **naturalization** records.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth AND the Oklahoma State Archives.
- Not confirmed as digitized in this survey — in-person or written request likely required.

### ✝️ Church & Mission Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (123,456 people).
- Note: Congregations formed only sporadically from 1889, so records may be thin in the earliest years.

### 🪶 Tribal Rolls (Indian Territory — Separate Stream)
- Relevant if any family straddled the Land Run area and Indian Territory.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" (567,890 people).
- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets**, 1898–1910: Browse-only images (0% indexed), held on FamilySearch.

### 💍 Marriage Records
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (available on FamilySearch).

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Land records, tribal rolls, marriages, church records | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Homestead patents and case files | Free |
| **National Archives (Washington, D.C.)** | GLO homestead files (RG 49) | In-person or written request |
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Oklahoma Territory district court records, 1890–1907 | In-person or written request |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | Territorial district court records | In-person or written request |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | 1890 special territorial census; territorial and early state records | In-person or written request |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. federal census | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com / Chronicling America | Historical newspapers | Subscription / Free |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Records NOT Yet Online (as confirmed by this survey)
- Statewide civil vital records (births/deaths) for the territorial period — civil registration is generally a post-1907 development.
- Oklahoma Territory district court case files at NARA Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives.
- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

---

## Known Record Losses
- No Oklahoma-specific record destruction was identified. The major national loss is the 1890 federal census (destroyed by fire/water damage) — the Oklahoma special territorial census survives as a valuable substitute.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with homestead files.** Land-entry case files are the richest source for Land Run settlers — they document family composition, witnesses, and settlement history.
2. **Search both record streams** if the family may have had ties to Indian Territory: use standard homestead/census records *and* Dawes Commission tribal rolls.
3. **Trace the family's origin state.** Since many settlers came from Kansas, Texas, or Missouri, their pre-1889 records will be in those states.
4. **Don't skip rejected claims.** Rejected homestead applications still survive and can contain important family details.
5. **Use the 1890 territorial census** as a substitute for the lost 1890 federal census.
6. **Tax rolls** from early 1890s county records can help document early settlers; held at the county level, not confirmed as digitized.

---

Oklahoma's Land Run records are largely federal (land and court) rather than state vital records, which barely existed yet in 1889–1907. The best starting points are the BLM's free General Land Office website for homestead patents, FamilySearch for indexed land and marriage collections, and the Oklahoma Historical Society for the surviving 1890 territorial census. For probate, naturalization, and civil records, contact the National Archives at Fort Worth or the Oklahoma State Archives directly.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory), c. 1798–1819

## Jurisdiction Overview

The land that became Alabama was **not yet its own place around 1800** — it was the western half of the **Mississippi Territory** (organized 1798), and the Mobile area remained under **Spanish colonial control until 1813**. It became the Alabama Territory in 1817 and the State of Alabama in 1819.

Settlement was concentrated around Mobile Bay and the Tennessee Valley/Tombigbee River areas. Much of the interior was held by Creek and Cherokee nations throughout this period. The Creek War (1813–1814) opened the interior to American settlement and triggered a wave of migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia.

---

## ⚠️ Key Research Warning: Search Under "Mississippi," Not Just "Alabama"

Because this area was part of Mississippi Territory until 1817, **all pre-statehood records are filed under Mississippi Territory jurisdiction** on FamilySearch. Searching only under "Alabama" will miss most of the territorial-era records. Use both place names.

---

## Record Types Available

### Census Records
- **Mississippi Territory territorial censuses** were taken in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** and cover present-day Alabama. Per a FamilySearch wiki search snippet (not a confirmed full-page read), these are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History, Montgomery**.
- **Online indexed collections:**
  - *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* (FamilySearch collection id 2016756, 287,634 persons)
  - *Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890* (id 1927171, 198,340 persons) — this opens well before 1798 and covers the entire target period.

### Land Records
- Pre-1813 Mobile District grants were issued under French, British, or Spanish colonial authority; American-era territorial land was federal public land (General Land Office).
- **Online:** *Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907* (id 1919694, 312,450 persons) — opens exactly at territorial formation.
- **Colonial-era grants** (Spanish, French): Per a wiki search snippet (unconfirmed by a full page read), French colonial records are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence), and Spanish-era land grants are at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville), with copies at the **Library of Congress**. Microfilm copies of French colonial records are reportedly at **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

### Church Records
- The Mobile District has **Spanish colonial church registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials in Spanish) going back well before 1800. Per the wiki search snippet, these are held at the Archivo General de Indias and the Library of Congress.
- **Online:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (id 1986396, 156,789 persons) and *Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950* (id 2034891, 87,654 persons) — both overlap the target period from their start dates.

### Marriage Records
- **Online:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (id 1598408) — the earliest county-level coverage begins 1809.

### Probate / Court Records
- **Online:**
  - *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (id 1537764, 438,210 persons)
  - *Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920* (id 1855293, 245,670 persons) — this series opens inside the 1798–1819 window and is the strongest match for territorial-era probate.

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- No territorial civil registration (birth/death) has been confirmed for this period. Church records and compiled census substitutes serve as the primary alternative sources.

---

## Digitized, Browsable (Non-Indexed) Volumes

Your specific question: **No digitized, browsable record volumes for this place and period were found.** Both `volume_search` and `catalog_search` returned **zero results** for "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" for 1798–1819. This is a digitization/coverage gap — the underlying records may exist physically but have not been digitized as browsable image sets that this survey could locate.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Indexed collections for marriages (1809+), probate (1809+), census substitutes (1792+), church records (1800+), land records (1798+), court records (1799+) — filed under both "Alabama" and "Mississippi" | Free |
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 (snippet claim — verify directly) | Contact repository |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville | Spanish-era Mobile District church registers, census returns, land grants (snippet claim) | Contact repository |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer**, Aix-en-Provence | French colonial records 1702–1763 (snippet claim) | Contact repository |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish-era Mobile District records (snippet claim) | Free (online/in-person) |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm copies of French colonial records (snippet claim) | Contact repository |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal originals: land patents, military service/pension records, naturalizations | Free (online/in-person) |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search both "Alabama" and "Mississippi" on FamilySearch** — the most important pre-statehood land and court collections are filed under "Mississippi."
2. **The Mobile District is a separate research trail** — Spanish-colonial Mobile records predate U.S. jurisdiction entirely, involve Spanish-language originals, and must be pursued through Spanish and French archives.
3. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama (Genealogy, Land and Property, Church Records) and the Mississippi Territory page all returned only a generic fallback during this survey — browse them directly at familysearch.org/wiki to see the full content.
4. Claims about the 1801–1810 territorial censuses and colonial-era archive holdings come from a **search snippet only** (not a confirmed full page read) — verify these leads by reading the full "Alabama Genealogy" FamilySearch wiki article before committing research time to them.
5. No pre-1819 civil vital registration was found — church records and census substitutes are your best alternatives for births and deaths in this period.

No tool result in this survey stated that any specific record set for this place and period was destroyed or lost. This absence of evidence is not evidence of survival or loss — it was not addressed by any page this survey could read.

## Research tips
- Every FamilySearch Wiki page this survey attempted for this place and period — Alabama's own Genealogy, Land and Property, and Church Records pages; the Mississippi Territory Genealogy page; and all four standard overview/getting-started/online-records/research-tips sections for Alabama — returned only a generic, non-place-specific fallback page (titled "Genealogy Records" or "Genealogy Research Guide," URLs familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records and .../Genealogy_Research_Guide). These are leads from a search snippet, not confirmed facts; verify them by reading the full "Alabama Genealogy" wiki article directly.

Around the year 1800, the land that became Alabama was not yet its own place at all — it was the western part of the Mississippi Territory (and, near Mobile, still under Spanish rule until 1813), so old records from that time are filed under those earlier names, not "Alabama." This search found some already-searchable record collections on FamilySearch covering marriages, probate (wills and estates), compiled census substitutes, church records, and land records for Alabama and Mississippi, several of which start right around 1798-1810, but it found zero digitized photograph collections that are simply browsable page-by-page without a name index — and the official reference pages that would normally describe start dates and record losses for this specific area did not return usable, place-specific content during this check, so several claims (such as the 1801-1810 territorial censuses and the old French/Spanish Mobile-area archives) come from a search snippet only and should be verified directly. ---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860s–1890s)

**Primary focus: Schuylkill County, PA** — the core of the anthracite region where Irish immigrant miners concentrated during this period.

### Key Findings

**Church Records**
- Catholic parish registers are the most important source for Irish families. Schuylkill County parishes fell under the **Philadelphia diocese** throughout the 1860s–1890s period.
- Many Irish miners arrived as Famine-era (post-1845) immigrants; Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the most reliable vital record substitute before civil registration.

**Civil and County Records on FamilySearch**
- **Probate, naturalization, deed, and marriage records** have been digitized by FamilySearch — but most are **browse-only image volumes without a name index**, so direct page-by-page browsing or use of a full-text search agent will be needed.

**Specialized Coal-Region Resources**
- A **"Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index"** of coal-company payroll records exists, along with unusually rich **Molly Maguires-era court and Pinkerton detective records** that name large numbers of Irish miners and their families. These are particularly valuable for the 1870s.
  - ⚠️ *Caveat: The payroll index's coverage of Schuylkill County collieries (vs. Lackawanna/Luzerne) is unconfirmed — verify before relying on it.*

**Civil Vital Registration**
- The exact year local birth/death registration began in Schuylkill County could not be confirmed from the wiki pages retrieved; Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906, but earlier county-level recording was inconsistent.

### Other Coal Counties
If your ancestor's trail extends beyond Schuylkill, separate locality guides should be built for:
- **Luzerne County** (Wilkes-Barre area)
- **Lackawanna County** (Scranton area — split from Luzerne in 1878)
- **Northumberland County**
- **Carbon County**

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Use the research plan to decide which record sets to search first (Catholic registers → naturalization → payroll records).
2. Build matching locality guides for the other four coal counties if the family's trail leads there.
3. For browse-only FamilySearch volumes, use the **search-images** agent to page through them or the **search-full-text** agent to query AI-transcribed documents.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Anthracite Coal Region (1860-1898)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811, from Berks and Northampton counties (place_search_all)
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** 1860: 89,510; 1870: 116,428; 1880: 129,974; 1900: 172,927 (US Census, via place_population)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; collieries employed large immigrant workforces
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish laborers dominated the workforce from the 1840s-1850s (post-Famine arrivals via Philadelphia); later joined by Eastern European immigrants (FamilySearch Wiki search result, Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic parishes established 1840-1870 to serve immigrant communities
- **Key historical events:** The Molly Maguires, a secret society active among Irish miners in the 1860s-1870s, generated extensive court records, trial transcripts, depositions and Pinkerton detective reports naming many Irish-born miners and families (FamilySearch Wiki search result, Schuylkill_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Molly_Maguires)

## Boundary changes
Schuylkill County has existed as a stable jurisdiction since its 1811 formation from Berks and Northampton counties (place_search_all: date_range "+1811/", no further splits recorded). Records before 1811 for this territory are in Berks or Northampton County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed this survey — the constructed Pennsylvania_Vital_Records wiki URL and all four wiki_place_page sections returned only a generic fallback page, not Pennsylvania-specific content. Do not assume a date; re-run this lookup before relying on a registration start year.
- **What exists:** A browse-only Marriage Records volume, 1870-1910, 94 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable (volume_search, imageGroupNumber 007936753).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized image volume (browse-only); county-level per volume_search.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death civil-registration volume surfaced in this survey for Schuylkill County.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptismal/burial registers (see Church records).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic parishes founded 1840-1870 for Irish and Eastern European immigrants (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (standard parish registers).
- **Where held:** Before 1868, all five anthracite counties (including Schuylkill) fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia. Schuylkill stayed with Philadelphia after 1868 (unlike Luzerne/Lackawanna, which moved to Scranton, and Northumberland, which moved to Harrisburg) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. A FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 007936751) holds Church Records, 1842-1895, 187 images, in English and German, 0% indexed, browse-only.
- **Gaps:** No name index for the 1842-1895 church-records volume; must browse image by image.
- **Language:** English and German (volume_search languages field); Catholic parish registers for Irish congregants may also be in Latin, not separately confirmed this survey.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Population recorded 1860-1900 (place_population); an 1850 Federal Census collection for Schuylkill County is externally linked via Ancestry (see Repository guide).
- **State/provincial census:** Not confirmed this survey.
- **Other enumerations:** Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments from 1853 list householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page) — useful as an intercensal substitute.
- **Access:** No federal census image volume specific to this county surfaced in volume_search; the Ancestry external link above is the confirmed federal-census access point.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories (standard county probate series); Molly Maguire-era trial transcripts, depositions, and detective reports also survive as court records naming Irish miners.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for Patrick Flynn in this survey — determine from his probate's own classification before searching a specific series.
- **Date range:** A Probate Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936749) covers 1851-1930, 412 images, 0% indexed, browse-only. A separate "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" collection (id 1999196) is indexed statewide but shows 0 persons indexed for this place in collections_search.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images (browse-only); county courthouse for originals.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed this survey (no Land_and_Property wiki page retrieved — only the generic fallback).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed.
- **Types:** Deed Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936752), 1815-1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed (partial), not full-text searchable.
- **Date range:** 1815-1900.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images, partially indexed; county recorder of deeds for originals.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War (1861-1865) falls within the target window.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, draft registrations — generic guidance only this survey; no Schuylkill-specific military volume surfaced.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA); Pennsylvania state archives for state militia/adjutant-general records.

### Cemetery records
- Not confirmed this survey — no FindAGrave/BillionGraves-specific link surfaced in external_links_search for this place.

### Newspaper records
- Not confirmed this survey — no newspaper-specific collection or link surfaced.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the chief port of arrival for Famine-era Irish immigrants to this region (FamilySearch Wiki search result).
- **Record types:** A Naturalization Records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936750) covers 1849-1915, 298 images, 0% indexed, browse-only.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch digitized images, browse-only; original naturalization petitions at the county court of record (pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record).
- **Content note:** Passenger-list manifests, when located, list every person aboard, including infant children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Pennsylvania state triennial assessments from 1853, listing householder, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity.
- **Date range:** Triennial from 1853 onward (Pennsylvania Coal Region Records wiki page).
- **Where held:** Not specified by the wiki page this survey; an Ancestry external link covers an earlier window, "Pennsylvania, U.S., Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768-1801" (outside this guide's 1860-1898 target period, listed for completeness).
- **Substitute value:** Fills gaps between the 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 federal censuses.

### Other record types — Coal-region specialized indexes

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (pre-statehood, c. 1770–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Admitted to Union:** 1791 (14th state). Before that, the territory was contested between New York and New Hampshire, each issuing competing land grants — the root of the "New Hampshire Grants" dispute.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Disputed between New York and New Hampshire colonial/state authority until Vermont operated as an independent republic (1777–1791), then was admitted to the United States.

---

## Boundary Changes
- Before 1791, there was no single civil authority. Both New York and New Hampshire granted land in this territory, and records from this era may be filed under those jurisdictions rather than "Vermont."
- The FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont Genealogy page notes a key pre-statehood resource: the **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**, prepared under New York colonial authority, listing ~1,800 grantees of disputed New Hampshire grants, including township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Statewide civil registration** did not begin until **1857** (per the FamilySearch Wiki Vermont Genealogy page).
- For 1770–1791, **some town clerk records survive from as early as the 1770s**, but survival is uneven and town-by-town — no statewide series exists for this period.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; not centralized.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule.

### Church Records
- Denominations, founding dates, and record locations were not addressed in detail by the pages retrieved. Church registers often predate civil registration by decades and should be checked at both the local parish and denominational archive level — but no Vermont-specific church collection was confirmed by this survey.

### Census Records
- The **1790 U.S. Federal Census** is the only federal enumeration that falls within the target window, and is the earliest federal census overall.
- No Vermont-specific state/territorial census, tax list, or other count was identified in this survey.

### Land Records
- **Most valuable record for this period:** The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — prepared under New York colonial authority, listing ~1,800 grantees of disputed New Hampshire grants, with grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and claim status.
- Because both New York and New Hampshire issued competing grants, search records under **both jurisdictions**, not just "Vermont."
- **19th-century Vermont town histories** (mostly published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records otherwise hard to access — a useful substitute source for 1770s–1780s land history.

### Military Records
- The Revolutionary War (ending 1783) falls within this window. Service records, pension files, and bounty-land warrants for this era are held at the **National Archives (NARA)** — but no Vermont-specific collection was confirmed by this survey.

### Probate and Court Records
- Not addressed with Vermont-specific detail in the pages retrieved. Likely held at town and county offices, but specific holdings were not confirmed.

### Cemetery, Newspaper, Tax, and Immigration Records
- None of these record types were addressed by any Vermont-specific tool result in this survey. They should be treated as likely physical-only or not yet discovered online — not as nonexistent.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | What it covers | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch Wiki – Vermont Genealogy | 1771 Grant Survey Schedule; town clerk vital records guidance; town histories | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census (incl. 1790) | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | Military/pension records for Revolutionary War era | Free (in-person/request) |
| Find A Grave | General cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |

> **Coverage note:** FamilySearch collections searches, volume searches, and catalog searches all returned zero results for Vermont in this survey. This is a confirmed gap in what this survey retrieved — not a statement that FamilySearch holds no digitized Vermont material. A narrower sub-place search (a specific town or county) is recommended before concluding nothing exists online.

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Individual Vermont town clerk offices | Town-level vital records surviving unevenly from the 1770s; contact each town directly |
| New York and New Hampshire state archives | Pre-statehood land-grant records issued by each colonial/state authority |

---

## Records NOT Online (as confirmed by this survey)
- Statewide/town-level pre-1791 vital records are not shown to be digitized or indexed online; the FamilySearch Wiki directs researchers to contact town clerks directly.
- No probate, court, tax, newspaper, or cemetery collection specific to pre-statehood Vermont was returned — treat these as likely physical-only or undiscovered-online for now.

## Known Record Losses
- No tool result in this survey identified any specific Vermont record series as destroyed or lost.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** for any ancestor who may have held or disputed a New Hampshire-granted township lot — it predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory.

2. **Go directly to town clerk offices** for vital records in this period. Because statewide registration didn't begin until 1857, town-level records (some dating to the 1770s) are your best option — but each town must be contacted individually; there is no centralized state index.

3. **Search under two jurisdictions.** Pre-statehood Vermont land was granted by two competing authorities (New York and New Hampshire). Search both jurisdictions' record systems, not just "Vermont," to find land and legal records for this period.

4. **Use 19th-century Vermont town histories** as a substitute source. Published mostly 1860–1900, they often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access.

5. **Don't overlook the 1790 Federal Census.** It's the only federal enumeration that falls within the target window (Vermont was admitted in 1791) and is the earliest federal census overall.

6. **Treat pre-statehood and post-statehood Vermont records as separate research tracks.** The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly warns researchers not to confuse pre-statehood land records with later post-statehood ones.

---

**Summary:** Vermont in the years 1770–1791 had no unified government systematically recording vital events, and civil registration didn't begin statewide until 1857. The most useful record for this early period is the 1771 land-grant survey listing ~1,800 grantees. Town-level birth, marriage, and death records exist in scattered form at individual town clerk offices, and church records likely fill further gaps. Land records will be split between New York and New Hampshire naming conventions. Much of what survives for this era is probably only on paper at town offices or not yet indexed online. A research plan targeting specific towns and record types is the recommended next step.

Here is the locality guide for **Yorkshire, England (1851)**, written to your project as **loc_001**:

---

## Yorkshire, England — Locality Guide for 1851

### Key Record for Finding a Death

**Civil Death Registrations** are the primary source. England and Wales began civil (government) registration of births, marriages, and deaths in **1 July 1837**, so by 1851 there is a well-established GRO (General Register Office) index. Each death was registered in the local registration district and an index entry created.

**How to search:**
- **FreeBMD** (freebmd.org.uk) — free searchable index of GRO records; best starting point
- **FamilySearch** — also indexes GRO vital records and is freely searchable
- **GRO (gro.gov.uk)** — order the original death certificate once you have the reference number; it names the informant, cause of death, and address

---

### Supporting Records

| Record Type | What It Provides | Where Held / How to Search |
|---|---|---|
| **1851 Census** (taken 30 March 1851) | Household, address, age, birthplace | FamilySearch, Ancestry, FindMyPast |
| **Church Burial Registers** | Burial date and parish; predates and supplements civil registration | Borthwick Institute for Archives (York); many on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| **Local Newspapers** | Death notices, obituaries | British Newspaper Archive (Findmypast); local library microfilm |
| **Monumental Inscriptions** | Headstone dates and family relationships | Local FHS (family history society) transcriptions |
| **Probate Records** | Date of death implicit in grant of probate | Borthwick Institute; National Probate Calendar (online) |

---

### Critical Yorkshire Geography Note ⚠️

Yorkshire was historically divided into **three Ridings**:
- **North Riding**
- **East Riding**
- **West Riding**

Many record collections — especially registration district indexes and historical transcriptions — are filed under the individual Riding name rather than "Yorkshire" as a whole. When searching, check both "Yorkshire" and the specific Riding for the town or village you're researching.

---

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Search FreeBMD** for the name in the GRO death index (1851 = Q1–Q4 volumes)
2. **Check the 1851 census** to place the person geographically before their death
3. **Search FamilySearch** for Yorkshire church burial registers if the civil index yields no result
4. If you identify a registration district, **order the GRO death certificate** for the full detail

The **research-plan** step can take this guide and lay out the actual search sequence for your specific individual. Let me know the name and any known details to proceed.

# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Ancient county, standardized by FamilySearch as "Yorkshire, England" 866-1801 and "Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom" from 1801 (place_search).
- **County seat / administrative center:** York (per collections such as "England, Yorkshire, York, Miscellaneous City Records").
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this standardPlace/period in this survey -- a coverage gap, not a statement of zero population.
- **Administrative note:** Yorkshire was historically divided into three Ridings (North, East, West), reflected in separate FamilySearch/Ancestry collections for "West Yorkshire" and "North Yorkshire" as well as county-wide "Yorkshire" collections.

## Boundary changes
- place_search shows two standardized representations: "Yorkshire, England" (866-1801) and "Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom" (1801-present); 1851 falls under the latter.
- Internally, the Riding structure (North/East/West) is the operative division for locating many record series -- a search of "Yorkshire" alone will miss Riding-specific collections.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration of deaths for England and Wales is indexed from 1837 in FamilySearch's "England and Wales, Death Registration Index 1837-2007" (collection 2285341, collections_search), so a death in 1851 falls within the civil registration period; FamilySearch's England_Vital_Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey and did not supply a Yorkshire-specific confirmation -- verify level/start date directly with GRO/GENUKI.
- **What exists:** "England and Wales, Death Registration Index 1837-2007" (87,352,096 people); "England and Wales, Index to Death Duty Registers, 1796-1903" (3,377,366 people, collection 4114269) for estates/probate-linked deaths.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (GRO) indexes, searchable via FamilySearch and FreeBMD (external_links_search: https://www.freebmd.org.uk/search) and findmypast's "England & Wales Deaths, 1837-2007" filtered to Yorkshire.
- **Gaps:** No Yorkshire-specific civil-registration volume was returned by volume_search or catalog_search in this survey.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Parish burial registers (see Church records) for deaths before or alongside 1837 civil registration.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England (parish registers, bishop's transcripts); Non-Conformist records also indexed for Yorkshire's West Riding.
- **Record types:** "England, Yorkshire, Parish Registers, 1538-2016" (collection 4439317, 27,344,590 people) includes burials; "England, Yorkshire, Bishop's Transcripts, 1547-1957" (collection 4319956, 11,853,270 people); Ancestry's "West Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1985" and "North Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1995" (external_links_search).
- **Where held:** Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York (external_links_search: http://www.york.ac.uk/borthwick/), which holds the Yorkshire diocesan/parish archive.
- **Gaps:** No tool result in this survey states a specific denomination or year range as lost for Yorkshire; none should be assumed.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **National census:** "England and Wales, Census, 1851" (collection 2563939, 1,569,726 people) directly covers the target year; 1841 and 1861 census collections also exist for context.
- **Access:** Indexed with person counts per collections_search; browsable via FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills and administrations; "Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858" (external_links_search, Ancestry collection 5246) covers 1851 pre-1858 (pre-Principal Probate Registry) probate, when probate was handled by ecclesiastical courts.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for this family; both will (testate) and administration (intestate) series should be checked.
- **Date range:** 1521-1858 for the Ancestry collection noted above; "England and Wales, National Index of Wills and Administrations, 1858-1957" applies after the 1858 reform.
- **Where held:** Borthwick Institute for Archives (ecclesiastical probate court records for the York diocese).

### Land records
- **Types:** "West Yorkshire, England, Select Land Tax Records, 1704-1932" (external_links_search, collection 5108).
- **Date range:** Covers 1851.
- **Where held:** Not specified by a tool result beyond the Ancestry collection; no FamilySearch catalog hit returned in this survey (catalog_search: 0 hits).

### Military records
- No Yorkshire-specific military collection was returned by any tool in this survey for 1851; the Crimean War (1853-56) postdates this death year.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** No FindAGrave/BillionGraves-specific Yorkshire 1851 collection appeared in results; "Yorkshire Monumental Inscriptions" (findmypast, external_links_search) is available.
- **Physical records:** Not detailed by tool results.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** "Yorkshire Gazette Newspaper Archives, 1819-1920" and "Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner, 1851-1982" (external_links_search, findmypast) both cover 1851 and could carry death/obituary notices.
- **Where held:** findmypast.com newspaper archive.

### Immigration/emigration records
- No Yorkshire-specific port/passenger record was returned by tool results for 1851; not a prime line of inquiry for an inland death record.

### Tax records
- **Types:** "West Yorkshire, England, Electoral Registers, 1840-1962" and "West Yorkshire, England, Select Rate Books, Accounts and Censuses, 1705-1893" (external_links_search).
- **Substitute value:** Rate books and electoral registers can corroborate residence around 1851 if vital records are inconclusive.

### Other record types
- Workhouse and Poor Law records exist for other English counties in collections_search results (e.g., Cheshire, Lancashire) but no Yorkshire-specific workhouse collection was returned in this survey; check GENUKI directly.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | England and Wales, Death Registration Index 1837-2007 (id 2285341); England and Wales, Census, 1851 (id 2563939); England, Yorkshire, Parish Registers, 1538-2016 (id 4439317); England, Yorkshire, Bishop's Transcripts, 1547-1957 (id 4319956) | Civil death index and 1851 census for the target year | Free |
| FreeBMD | GRO index search (https://www.freebmd.org.uk/search) | Free alternative civil-registration index lookup | Free |
| findmypast | England & Wales Deaths, 1837-2007 (filterable to Yorkshire); Yorkshire Gazette Newspaper Archives, 1819-1920; Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner, 1851-1982 | Death index cross-check and period newspaper obituaries | Subscription |
| Ancestry | West Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1985 (collection 2254); North Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1995 (collection 62238); Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858 (collection 5246) | Riding-specific burial registers and pre-1858 probate | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned 0 digitized-volume matches for Yorkshire, England 1840-1861, and catalog_search returned 0 catalog hits -- these tools did not surface further material beyond the collections and external links listed above.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Borthwick Institute for Archives, University of York | Diocesan/parish registers, ecclesiastical probate records | In-person/written request (http://www.york.ac.uk/borthwick/) |
| General Register Office (GRO), England and Wales | Original civil registration death certificates from 1837 | Order by post/online via GRO |

## Records NOT online
- Original civil death certificates are not themselves viewable online; only the GRO index is searchable online (FamilySearch, FreeBMD, findmypast) -- the full certificate must be ordered from the GRO.
- Physical probate records and estate files at the Borthwick Institute are not confirmed as digitized by any tool result in this survey.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey states that any Yorkshire vital, parish, or probate record series was destroyed or lost for the 1851 period; none should be assumed to be missing.

## Research tips
- Search both the county-wide "Yorkshire" collections and the Riding-specific "West Yorkshire"/"North Yorkshire" collections -- FamilySearch/Ancestry file many 19th-century series by Riding, not by the whole historic county (collections_search, external_links_search results).
- Cross-check the GRO civil death index (via FamilySearch's 2285341 or FreeBMD) against parish burial registers (collection 4439317) for the same name and year, since a civil index entry gives only name/quarter/district/volume/page, not cause or full details.
- Use the 1851 census (collection 2563939) to confirm the person was alive and resident in Yorkshire earlier in the year, narrowing which registration district's death index to search.
- Check period local newspapers (e.g., Yorkshire Gazette, Huddersfield and Holmfirth Examiner) for an obituary or death notice naming cause of death, survivors, or exact date.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's generic place pages and the England_Vital_Records page did not return Yorkshire-specific detail in this survey; consult GENUKI's Yorkshire page (http://www.genuki.org.uk/big/eng/YKS) and the Yorkshire BMD index (http://www.yorkshirebmd.org.uk/) directly for registration-district detail.
- If the person died testate, check "Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858" (pre-1858 ecclesiastical probate, Borthwick Institute); if intestate, the same series covers administrations too.
